SEATTLE - The family of a 29-year-old U.S. Coast Guard rescue pilot who was shot and killed in Skyway is offering a $30,000 reward for information leading to an arrest in the case.

Lt. Connor Overstreet was killed early Sunday, August 23, near South 124th Street and South Langston Road, according to the King County Sheriff’s Office. Deputies were dispatched at about 12:40 a.m. after receiving reports of a shooting.

The Medical Examiner’s Office determined Overstreet died from a gunshot wound to his chest.

No suspects have been identified, and the investigation remains ongoing.

Connor Overstreet, who was shot and killed on Aug. 23 in Skyway.

What they're saying:

Overstreet’s sister, Shea Overstreet, described him as kind, thoughtful and someone who made time for anyone who needed him.

"Connor was really the best of us," Shea Overstreet said. "He was my best friend."

Overstreet was an active-duty Coast Guard pilot assigned to Air Station Ventura in California. He was here visiting Washington state for work and training. His sister said he loved flying, the outdoors, his family and his two dogs, Harry and Kenai.

"Connor loved the Coast Guard. He loved flying. He loved the challenge and the community and all he wanted to do was to help people," she said. "He wanted to save lives more than anything else."

His wife, Madeleine, also described him as her best friend and her "rock," saying in a statement that he had dedicated his life to saving others.

"All Connor wanted to do was save lives by flying for the Coast Guard," she said.

Connor Overstreet

Dig deeper:

Detectives with the Sheriff’s Office Major Crimes Unit have been canvassing the area and are looking for surveillance or dashcam video recorded between 12:30 and 1:15 a.m. Investigators are particularly interested in video showing people or vehicles.

The community has rallied raising money to increase the Crime Stoppers reward to $30,000 for a tip that leads to an arrest in the case.

Right now, no information is insignificant as far as we know, this was a random act of gun violence," said his sister.

Map of where King County deputies are seeking video in an August 23 homicide, and a QR code to submit evidence. (King County Sheriff's Office)

Shea Overstreet said the family hopes the reward encourages someone with information to speak up.

"We know that nothing can bring him back, but if we could spare one other family or anybody from having to endure this pain and loss and devastation, we’ll do that for Connor," she said.

She also urged whoever knows what happened to come forward.

"Please help us," she said. 

Tips can be submitted anonymously through the P3 Tips app or at https://t.co/HAJHQVJ1ot. Tipsters also can call 1-800-222-TIPS (8477). Authorities say tipsters will not be asked to provide their names.

Shea Overstreet said the family is grateful for the support it has received as it grieves.

"Please just be kind to one another," she said. "That’s what Connor would have done. And give your loved ones one more hug,"

Before the strikes, the United States was running two tracks at once: talks in Oman and Geneva in February 2026, and preparations for military action. Reports from those sessions indicated movement on sanctions relief (as much as 80 percent in some accounts) and U.S. offers of imported nuclear fuel in exchange for limits on enrichment. The military threat remained unused and therefore still credible as a source of pressure, while Iran’s economy was already strained by sanctions and earlier 2025 strikes. That combination gave Washington room to demand longer restrictions or more verification without having already spent lives, munitions, and political capital. 
https://t.co/QfXdXH108F

Once the war began on 28 February 2026, those advantages evaporated. The campaign, which Trump initially described as a short “excursion,” lasted more than six months, cost more than $37 billion, produced U.S. casualties, and failed to collapse the Iranian government or eliminate its remaining highly enriched uranium stockpile. Iran responded by tightening control over the Strait of Hormuz, creating a new source of economic leverage that did not exist in the same form during the earlier talks. The June 2026 memorandum of understanding then offered Iran hundreds of billions in reconstruction funding and broad sanctions relief while leaving core nuclear questions (enrichment duration, disposition of 60-percent material, inspector access) for later negotiation; that framework quickly unraveled amid renewed fighting. 
https://t.co/EHUpFIJJ4o

By starting the war, Trump handed Iran enormous leverage. Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, and Trump has so far proved unable to restore the level of shipping that existed before the war. That gives Iran more bargaining power in any negotiation, not less.

In short, the credible threat of force was a stronger negotiating tool than the actual, inconclusive use of force.

Trump has now burned through much of America’s available munitions and strategic oil reserves while failing to achieve his central objectives. Instead of demonstrating American strength, he has made U.S. military power look less effective—and his own strategy look incompetent.

(Sorry, I went a little deep on this one…but you made me think about some of the most important men in my life, who are no longer here, with me. Thank you for that…their memory should be honored daily! Hope you don’t mind the long response!) 🙏🏼🫶🏼

This was one of my father’s least favorite things to do. 

It was one of my middle brother’s least favorite things to do. 

It is one of my youngest brother’s least favorite things to do. 

My father & middle brother were GCs. (RIP, I miss them dearly & I think about them constantly). 

My youngest brother is also a GC. 

The men in my family have been in this profession pretty far back. I’m sure they’d all support you in this conclusion. They’re also the type that is the first to arrive at the job site & the last to leave. They work with their employees instead of just standing there, expecting them to “take orders,” & do all the work. 

My family is responsible for rebuilding & the renovations of much of Washington DC (going back a century). I have things from the U.S. Capitol Building & SCOTUS Buildings, like: the original “chandeliers” that were initially installed, when they installed electricity in the Capitol Building, parts of the roof…which my grandfather made into lanterns, drapes, mounted light fixtures, & a few other items. 

My dad was really cool, though. In the 90s there were a lot of buildings, in downtown DC that were rundown, & had turned into (for lack of a better word) “trap-houses.” 

They were full of nothing but homeless people smoking crack & shooting-up heroin. My father would spend time speaking to many of those who were in each of the buildings he bought to fix-up & sell. He would then always pick 1-2 of them & make them an offer. 

They’d be allowed to remain on the property throughout the remainder of the project, but they had to remain clean. If they required going through detox initially…he would take care of that. Their responsibilities would be to ensure no one entered the property at night while the project was closed down & workers were not present. They were to choose one of the available trades he offered. He & his crew would teach them…they were responsible for learning their chosen trade. They were responsible for the “security” of the job site. He had all of their personal details, there were contracts signed & he had a way with these guys. 

If they were dependable & picked up the trade he taught…he would offer them a full-time position at the end of the project. He paid them throughout this, fair wages, provided them with meals each day, & provided them with an appropriate place to sleep & bathe on property. 

My father was a Vietnam Veteran who served his country as a United States Marine. He suffered from severe PTSD (he dealt with this alone for many years). Many of those he helped…they were veterans, as well. Ultimately, he passed from duty related injuries (it’s on his death certificate), that were left untreated until 2011. He really didn’t start getting adequate care for them until 2017. Can you imagine? Your country willfully choosing to ignore what happened to you for 50 years…when you chose to serve & defend?

My youngest brother, he also has a soft spot for those who are facing hard times. He will hire them, provide them with living arrangements, & help them to get back on their feet.

text:
A stronger RMB can squeeze Chinese exporters, but the real strain starts if Beijing has to keep replacing those lost margins with cheaper state credit.

Japan’s experience after Plaza matters less for how far the yen moved than for what happened once the stronger currency worked through banks, credit and asset prices. West Germany took a large appreciation too without following Japan down the same path, while Japan moved into aggressive easing in 1986 as financial liberalization gathered pace, sending credit into land and equities and helping its banks expand overseas at extraordinary speed.

Basel I tightened the constraint a few years later. Japanese banks carried relatively thin core capital, while unrealized equity gains could count toward Tier 2 — comfortable while stocks kept rising, much less so once the market turned.

China has adjusted through the exchange rate before, and the RMB appreciation after 2005 coincided with a large decline in its external surplus, so the currency still matters. Since then, though, much more of China’s advantage has accumulated in intermediate goods, machinery and deeply integrated supply chains.

A stronger RMB can push up the dollar price of Chinese exports, but it cannot move a supplier cluster, a port, a power grid and an engineering workforce 20% farther away. Even when Chinese factories move to Vietnam, Mexico or Hungary, plenty of the machinery, components and financing can still trace back to China.

If that industrial network stays put while margins get squeezed, Beijing can cushion the hit through state banks, local governments and policy funds for far longer than most countries could. Doing that repeatedly means supporting exporters while refinancing local governments, recapitalizing banks, absorbing property losses and keeping strategic capacity alive, all through overlapping pools of public credit and balance-sheet capacity.

Capital controls buy Beijing even more time because much of the stress sits in RMB debt, giving China far more room than Korea had in 1997 and making a sudden IMF-style replay much harder. The losses do not disappear, though; property debt, LGFVs and industrial support keep feeding back into the same banks and public balance sheets.

China spent decades studying Japan after Plaza and Korea in 1997, then built a system designed to make both outcomes harder to reproduce. That changes the American game as well, because Washington does not necessarily need to break the system if repeated pressure keeps forcing Beijing to use it, burning more money, more credit and more balance-sheet capacity each time another exporter, strategic industry, local government or asset market needs support.

As that capacity gets scarcer, weaker firms are more likely to be cut loose while stronger firms, SOEs and local champions absorb assets and market share. The first phase could therefore leave Beijing with even more state control, while concentrating more of the financing burden inside the same system and forcing it to spend more to defend fewer positions.

Washington pays for the pressure too through higher import costs, supply-chain disruption and strain on allies, so this only works as an attrition strategy if Beijing is forced to spend more defending the system than the U.S. spends pressuring it.

Foreign equity, market access and financial opening would come later, if restructuring eventually leaves Beijing needing capital or concessions it would rather not offer. Korea showed how quickly those terms can change once balance sheets force action, while China built its capital controls and state banking system precisely to keep that moment from arriving on somebody else’s timetable.

China studied Japan and Korea and built the fortress accordingly, but every hit it absorbs costs Beijing more to hold the walls.

To wit:

“We have inherited this island.”

So this is a soft ‘we’ being employed here, and as to all the adepts of Critical Race Theory its use is two fold, it’s declarative in the sense that the historic people are expected to accept this declarative ‘we’ as the new baseline and it’s simultaneously transformative, the effect in the collective consciousness is an attempt to detach ownership from any ancient primordial historic lineage and reconnect it to a distributed open source all things to all people multi-node (the soft ‘we’) model situated permanently in the gestalt/present.

“Every generation inherits a country and redefines it.”

text:
Adam Bandt’s Bird-Brained Climate Theory
by @JamesMacpherson [COMMENTARY]

Climate change isn’t just a theory — it’s the Greens’ universal scapegoat.

Adam Bandt may not be leading the Greens anymore, but that doesn’t mean he’s given up lecturing the nation on the evils of coal and gas.

And he doesn’t need much of an excuse. Literally any reason will do.

So with the arrival of bird flu, naturally, Adam Bandt saw an opportunity to sermonise on fossil fuels.

“It’s really distressing. Like I bet you’re upset. I am too. Watching the spread of bird flu over recent weeks, it’s just been incredibly devastating.

“One of the things that this has really brought home is that it is time to stop already vulnerable populations under even more pressure by habitat destruction and climate change.”

Just one problem.

Bird flu is not caused by climate change.

But I get the temptation. Honestly, I do.

Climate change has become the Swiss Army knife of political explanations. Whatever the problem, simply unfold the climate-change blade and start waving it around…

Scientists have blamed climate change for bumpy Jetstar flights.

The ACT Government has blamed climate change for potholes.

And the World Health Organisation has blamed climate change for bad hair days.

So why not add birds with the Influence A virus to the list of casualties?

“Now is the time to stop bulldozing their habitat. Now is the time to stop opening new coal and gas mines pushing climate change even worse and making already vulnerable populations take that one step closer to extinction.”

If Adam Bandt is genuinely worried about bulldozing habitat, he might want to have a word with the renewable-energy industry.

Because there is an awkward little problem with the Greens’ vision of an all-electric, all-renewable utopia: wind and solar infrastructure does not simply materialise on pristine land after being delivered by a particularly eco-friendly fairy.

It requires roads, transmission infrastructure, substations, construction and, in many cases, the clearing and fragmentation of habitat.

Perhaps Bandt could explain why bulldozing bushland for renewable energy is virtuous, while bulldozing bushland for anything else is an unforgivable sin.

And then came the grand finale:

“We have a really significant opportunity right here, right now to offer the best protection to our wildlife, and that means stop habitat destruction and stop making climate change worse.”

There’s something almost touching about Bandt’s confidence that Australia possesses a giant planetary thermostat hidden somewhere underneath Parliament House.

Apparently, if Australia stops opening coal and gas mines, the world’s climate will breathe a sigh of relief, and bird flu will reconsider its travel arrangements.

The reality is rather less convenient.

Australia should absolutely protect wildlife habitat.

It should absolutely take bird flu seriously.

And it should absolutely scrutinise any development — renewable or otherwise — that threatens important habitat.

But turning a bird-virus outbreak into another advertisement for the climate agenda isn’t environmental leadership.

It is opportunism with feathers.

Bandt doesn’t appear to understand that bird flu isn’t caused by climate change, that renewable infrastructure can itself have environmental impacts, or that Australia alone cannot meaningfully control global temperatures by refusing to develop another coal or gas project.

But at least he has managed to find one thing that apparently has an easier time spreading than bird flu. And that’s a climate change talking point.

Read the full piece at https://t.co/xM7tKuOIBF

text:
Then the food started arriving.

Wild Mushroom Tartine with citrus crème fraîche, pickled onions and Espelette honey. The thing was huge. Rich, savory, crisp, a little sweet and gone almost immediately.

Next, the cup of Onion Soup Gratinée.

They offer two sizes, which is genius. Sometimes you want molten cheese and deeply caramelized onions without committing to a cereal bowl of it.

The cup was perfection in a cup.

The menu’s Scallop Risotto became Snapper Risotto for us, and holy hell.

Crisp-skinned snapper over wildly creamy, decadent risotto with pistou, brown-butter crumb and Parmesan. Probably my favorite dish of the night.

The kitchen handled the substitution without turning it into a thing. No committee meeting. No menu drama. Just done.

I went traditional with Coq au Vin: roasted Green Circle chicken, shallots, mushrooms, carrots and pomme purée in a proper dark, rich sauce.

Exactly what I wanted. Classics survive for a reason.

Then the Cauliflower Gratinée.

We ordered cauliflower under the fiction that we were making one responsible decision. It arrived creamy, cheesy and completely ridiculous.

Apparently cauliflower just needed better management.

The beverage program is where Boulon really got me.

Leilani Jacobs, Boulon’s bar manager, listened to what we were eating and pulled an off-list Gramercy Cellars Viognier from Washington State.

Crisp, fun, a little unexpected and somehow right with the tartine, onion soup, snapper risotto and even the coq au vin.

That’s a strange assignment for one white wine. It handled all of it.

Because I am me, I also noticed the 2017 Dom Pérignon and remember thinking the restaurant pricing looked surprisingly sane.

We didn’t order it. I was just auditing Champagne markups like a completely normal person.

Naturally, I photographed the vintage but not the price. After 25,000 steps, my documentation department had closed.

(2/3)

32 TEAMS.

32 FANTASY QUESTIONS.

LOS ANGELES CHARGERS: WHICH RECEIVER STAYS ON THE FIELD?

Los Angeles enters 2026 with plenty of reasons to like the offense.

The Chargers are projected for 23.8 points per game, 13th in the NFL, and their offensive line ranks ninth in the guide's 2026 aggregate ranking. Justin Herbert is entering his prime, while the return of Rashawn Slater and Joe Alt gives the offense a healthier foundation.

The bigger change is Mike McDaniel taking over as offensive coordinator.

His Miami offenses leaned heavily on motion, 21 personnel and running-back involvement. The guide expects the Chargers to follow that direction, potentially challenging for the league lead in heavy personnel usage.

That creates a very specific fantasy question:

Which wide receivers will actually stay on the field when Los Angeles uses two-receiver sets?

Ladd McConkey has the clearest answer. The guide views him as a near lock to remain on the field in heavy personnel, which could give him a significant advantage over his competition.

Quentin Johnston and Tre' Harris present a less certain situation.

Johnston offers a physical deep-threat profile but provides little as a blocker. Harris brings the opposite skill set and could earn more snaps than the market currently expects because of what McDaniel values from his receivers.

That matters because the Chargers had the league's No. 1 wide receiver target share last season at 68.7%.

The offense may continue producing plenty of receiver fantasy points, but the distribution could change significantly if McDaniel increases the use of heavier personnel.

When drafting a Charger, we should look beyond the projected passing volume and ask which players have a role that survives the formation changes.

For McConkey, that consistency is part of the appeal. For the other receivers, we're making a more specific bet about who wins the snaps that remain available.

32 TEAMS.

32 FANTASY QUESTIONS.

LAS VEGAS RAIDERS: WHO EMERGES BEHIND BOWERS?

The Raiders scored just 14.2 points per game last season, dead last in the NFL.

That makes the passing game difficult to trust at first glance. But Las Vegas changed the environment around it, bringing in Klint Kubiak and Kirk Cousins while adding Jalen Nailor to a receiver room that already included Tre Tucker and Jack Bech.

Brock Bowers is the clear centerpiece.

His 84% route participation ranked third among tight ends in 2025, but he averaged only 34.1 routes per game. The guide sees room for that number to increase in Year 3, particularly with very little added competition for targets.

That leaves us with a more interesting question than whether Bowers will be good.

Who captures the passing production behind him?

The Raiders have three receivers competing for that role. Tre Tucker and Jalen Nailor are being drafted around WR64-70, while Jack Bech is essentially free in drafts.

The guide doesn't give us a definitive answer either.

Tucker and Nailor have the market's attention, but the analysis points toward Bech as an intriguing alternative because his skill set may fit what Kubiak's offense asks from its receivers. With the hierarchy behind Bowers still wide open, there are multiple paths to upside.

That matters for how we approach this offense in drafts.

We don't need to correctly predict which receiver becomes the clear No. 2 before the season starts. We need to recognize that the market is pricing several players as though the hierarchy is already settled.

In Best Ball especially, that creates an opportunity to take inexpensive shots at the same unresolved role.

When drafting a Raider, the question isn't simply whether the offense improves.

It's which players can capture the additional opportunity if it does—and whether we're paying for that outcome before the hierarchy has actually been established.

text:
What your parents never told you:

Based on a careers barrier to entry, its salary could be called 'Economical'-
Even if the pay gap is huge, an $80K/y casino dealer is = $160K surgeon, because the barrier to entry takes more time + skills.

Here are two lists of careers, starting from the lowest pay to the highest, of careers that are Economical and those that are Above Economical.

1. The Economical pay ladder, with the barriers that keeps each rung from flooding.

Around $100K - $120K: 
project managers, senior accountants, experienced nurses, mid-level engineers. 
The barrier is mostly experience and credentials — real, but supply still catches up over a decade, so pay stays near normal return.

$120K - $160K: 
specialized nurses, senior software engineers, experienced finance analysts. 
Now you’re adding scarce skills or location — tech hubs, hospital systems with limited residency pipelines.

$160K - $250K: physicians outside surgery, senior lawyers, quantitative analysts, airline captains. 
Licensing, years of training, and hard caps on supply — med school seats, bar passage rates, FAA limits.

$250K - $400K: surgeons, partners at big law firms, hedge fund managers, senior tech executives. 
The barrier is extreme — decades of training, tiny partnership slots, or performance that compounds.

>$400K: top surgeons, elite hedge fund managers, founders of successful companies. 
Here the barrier is often talent plus luck plus network effects, and the rent is huge because supply is nearly fixed.

2. Above-economical 

Meaning the barrier is so strong that supply never catches up — the rent sticks around for decades.

$100K - $120K: specialized trades in boom regions — oilfield welders in the Permian, union electricians in California. Licensing exists, but demand outruns training capacity, so wages sit above normal return.

$120K - $160K: nurse anesthetists, physician assistants in underserved areas, senior cloud architects. The training is shorter than a doctor’s, but the credential is scarce and demand keeps climbing.

$160K - $250K: radiologists, anesthesiologists, patent attorneys, senior derivatives traders. Residency slots and exam pass rates are hard caps — you can’t just train more people fast enough.

$250K - $400K: orthopedic surgeons, partners at top law firms, quant researchers at hedge funds. The barrier is decades plus tiny intake — a handful of fellowship spots, a handful of partnership offers a year.

> $400K: neurosurgeons, elite hedge fund managers, founders of scaled software companies. Here the rent is enormous because the barrier is nearly impenetrable — talent, network, and luck all compounding.

text:
Podcast Summary | The Diary Of A CEO with Steven Bartlett: Top White House Advisor: The US Empire Is DYING And Socialism Is Coming Next! | David Friedberg

Overview

David Friedberg, a scientist, entrepreneur, and member of President Trump's science and technology advisory council, presents a stark diagnosis of America's current condition. He argues that the US is an empire in decline, facing an unaffordability crisis where 63% of Americans live paycheck to paycheck. He believes that a wave of socialism is absolutely inevitable, driven by national debt, government dependency, and wealth inequality. However, Friedberg is not a pessimist; he is a fierce advocate for individual agency, capitalism, and technological progress. He sees AI as a golden age that will expand the economy and create new opportunities, not destroy jobs. His core prescription is to fix the tax code to address inequality without seizing assets, reform government incentives to curb short-termism, and trust in the historical power of free markets and individual liberty to solve our problems.

Key Themes

- The US empire is in decline, marked by economic distress where 63% of Americans live paycheck to paycheck and costs outpace wages, a condition that historically leads to internal strife and external conflict.
- A shift toward socialism is inevitable because of compounding national debt, Federal Reserve policy, and roughly half the population relying on government employment or benefits.
- AI is a golden age and the most important subject of our time; it will not cause mass unemployment because technological revolutions have historically increased jobs and incomes by boosting productivity.
- The tax code, not capitalism, is the root of wealth inequality; capital gains compound untaxed while labor is taxed every paycheck, making a flat tax on capital the solution.
- The American Dream is not homeownership but the transition from labor to capital, moving from living on paychecks to living on asset income.
- Government expansion is a failure; services it touches, like education and housing, become more expensive, and the great lie is that the government will save you.
- Open-source AI models are a hedge against wealth concentration, offering a path for new billionaires to emerge from nowhere and challenging the dominance of big tech players.
- A policy shift toward the "Denmark model" of high taxes and social services would erode the liberty and incentives that drive American progress, a tradeoff that is likely unsolvable.

Detailed Summary

Friedberg frames the American condition as an empire in decline, pointing to Ray Dalio's "cycle of empires" theory, which tracks the rise and fall of six empires over 500 years, with the US declining and China rising. He connects this internal economic distress to foreign policy, claiming that unhappy nations go to war, while happy nations do not. The unaffordability crisis is central to this decline; with 63% of Americans having less than $500 in savings, the social fabric is strained. This economic pain, he argues, makes a wave of socialism inevitable, as a majority of Americans become reliant on government employment or support.

Friedberg’s primary enemy is not capitalism but a flawed tax policy. He explains that labor is taxed on every paycheck, while capital gains are only taxed when an asset is sold, allowing wealth to compound tax-free. This creates an inherent advantage for asset holders. His proposed fix is to tax capital at the same rate as labor, ideally at the moment of transaction. He strongly rejects a wealth tax, calling it an "asset seizure" that is antithetical to the US founding principle of private property rights and likely unconstitutional under the Fifth Amendment. He cites France's failed wealth tax, which drove wealthy individuals out of the country and reduced total tax revenue, as evidence.

Friedberg elaborates on how the wealthy avoid taxes through borrowing. Banks offer loans against stock holdings at low interest rates, allowing individuals to fund large purchases without selling assets and triggering a taxable event. He frames this as a loophole that should be a taxable event. He also dismantles the "great American dream" of homeownership, calling it a "great lie" that concentrates capital in one asset and inflates prices, making homes unaffordable for younger generations while enriching existing owners. He suggests that investing in the S&P 500, which averages 10-11% annual returns, is a more effective path to building wealth.

The speaker’s core philosophy is that individual agency, not government intervention, is the solution to economic hardship. He advises young people to ask themselves, "What did you do today that someone else valued?" and to repeat that. He points to the internet as an unprecedented enabler for new income paths, from podcasting to online selling. The host pushes back, noting that government infrastructure like free schooling, healthcare, and a social safety net provided the stable foundation that enabled his own risk-taking. Friedberg acknowledges the tension, arguing that the goal is a balance between government dependency and a universal entrepreneur path, focusing on an individual's capacity to create value.

On AI, Friedberg is unwaveringly optimistic. He argues that technological revolutions have never led to net job loss, citing the shift from farming to factory work and the panic over computers in the 1960s and 1980s. He sees AI as a tool for creative leverage, enabling one person to do the work of a team. He counters the idea of a "fixed pie" economy, asserting that automation expands the economy and benefits workers over time. He predicts that AI will compress routine knowledge work, freeing up time for other value creation, and that in-person experiences will become more valuable as automation handles routine tasks.

Friedberg is critical of AI leaders who warn of existential risk, pointing to their inconsistent narratives. He cites Sam Altman's shift from calling AI the "greatest threat to humanity" in 2015 to later reassuring the public, and Elon Musk's 2014 warning about "summoning the demon." He also disputes the narrative that AI is causing job losses, using Klarna as an example. While Klarna's founder confirmed he is cutting staff due to AI, the company's revenue doubled, and it rehired for VIP services. Friedberg argues that cost savings enable companies to invest in new products, which drives hiring. The real question, he insists, is not whether to slow AI development, which is "too far too late," but where data centers and models are built—domestically or offshore.

Friedberg champions open-source AI as a tool against wealth concentration. He notes that Chinese open-source models can be as good as or better than private American models at a fraction of the cost. He dismisses concerns about Chinese models as backdoor programs, explaining that they are just "a list of numbers." He predicts that within a decade, a new billionaire will emerge from building a company on open-source AI, challenging the idea that big players like Elon Musk or Sam Altman will capture all the value.

Finally, Friedberg addresses the fear of socialism by outlining his vision for a better path. He calls for term limits for politicians and a rotation between public and private life to combat the short-termism of four-year election cycles. He argues that the choice for America is between "inequality or lack of progress," using the "golden goose" analogy to illustrate that while early adopters of technology race ahead, value eventually diffuses to everyone. He rejects the "Denmark model" of high taxes and universal services, arguing that it would erode the freedom and incentives that drive entrepreneurial risk-taking and frontier progress, like life-saving CART-T cancer therapies. He believes the answer is not to confiscate wealth from the top, but to enable the bottom 50% to build capital and achieve the transition from labor to capital themselves.

There is no redeeming value in the use of their product except individual smokers say the "benefits" of smoking to them are that it helps regulate mood, relieve stress, bond socially and some even cite weight control as a benefit. The medical harm, however, is almost universal and well documented. But the tech companies’ cases are different.

Every medicine comes with warning about side effects. Among millions who may use a particular medicine, a few people are bound to suffer side effects because everyone’s body is different. The same is the case with vaccines. Global immunization efforts have saved an estimated 154 million lives over the past 50 years. A study led by the World Health Organization (WHO) and published in The Lancet revealed that the vast majority of these lives saved—146 million—were children under the age of five, including 101 million infants under one year old.

In the U.S. alone, data tracking 30 cohorts of children born between 1994 and 2023 shows that routine immunizations prevented over 1.1 million deaths and saved $2.7 trillion in societal costs.

Severe injury or death directly caused by modern vaccines is extraordinarily rare, occurring in fewer than one to two cases per million doses administered. In most prominent instances of vaccines directly causing widespread death or paralysis occurred decades ago due to early manufacturing and safety failures that led to modern, highly strict quality controls.

Thus, medicines and vaccines have done a tremendous amount of good for humanity. In extremely rare cases children or adults may suffer permanent injury or in rare cases even death. But that is no justification for bankrupting the medicine and vaccine manufacturers or making it unprofitable for them to manufacture vaccines.

The tech companies are doing an enormous amount of good for humanity, especially by providing most of their services for free. That’s why 3.6 billion individuals, about 45% of the world’s population use Meta’s products alone. If we consider the approximately 6.9 billion people above the age of 9 who can possibly use Meta products, then about 52% of people in the world use them. If we leave the illiterate or people too poor to afford a smartphone, then probably above 80% humanity capable of using them uses Meta products. So many users use the services provided free in most cases because they derive a lot of joy and other tremendous benefits from using them. How ridiculous does the argument that the product itself is defective sound.

Social media (SM) has benefited humanity tremendously by transforming global communications, bridging distances globally, enabling building of close bonds with family and friends and maintaining them, reduced isolation, democratized knowledge and learning so that its possible to learn almost anything new for free, allowed small businesses to flourish by enabling them to communicate with a massive number of potential and actual customers at little or no cost, make disaster response quick and efficient and in many other ways. Social media is not a defective product.

I as a user, am happy that “Reels” show up in my feed, the kind I like viewing the most. I watch some. If I have more time, I watch a few more without having to perform a search each time. But if I don’t have the time, I just shut it off. I view the continuous feed of content I like as a benefit.

As stated earlier, the correct approach should be to hold discussions with companies whenever problems are detected with their products and services, confirmed by sufficient evidence. Conduct further studies as necessary, funded primarily by the companies. The studies should result in recommendations for changes such as those imposed on Meta in the settlement without the company having to pay fines and penalties after the fact. If the company refuses to enact such changes, only then lawsuits should be filed against the companies. But, when one is dealing with humanity, this is always going to be a work in progress. There is no reason to grab the cash of the companies or bankrupt them.

I think it’s unfair for school districts to sue social media companies. They have the authority to restrict use of cell phones in their schools during school time as some schools have started doing. They should come up with such solutions to tackle any problems during school time rather than alleging that the product is addictive because it is defective.

Since we are dealing with human beings, more challenges in the form of possible harmful effects should be expected. It will always be a work in progress. That means a public-private partnership is required to stay on top of issues and deal with them before they become major problems. In fact, such issues should be tackled globally since the products of SM companies are used globally. SM companies trade associations such as NetChoice and TechNet should work with foreign, federal and state regulators to actively resolve emerging issues. The 48 attorneys general have come up with recommendations after filing lawsuits against Meta. Since the Meta settlement with the 47 attorneys general has yet to be signed by a judge, the amount of the settlement should be reviewed in light of the legal arguments I have provided which were not put forth during the trial. At the very least, the $567 million into a youth harm abatement fund for New Mexico should be included as part of the settlement with the 47 attorneys general and settlement for similar expenditures with the state of Florida. In fact, the changes will be applied globally. Therefore, the same funds for youth harm abatement should be used globally so that foreign countries will have no justification for demanding additional compensation from the company.

In conclusion, there is no justification for treating Meta or other SM companies like the tobacco companies. SM company products are not defective products like the products of the tobacco companies. SM products are more like medicines and vaccines which do a tremendous amount of good for humanity, but a few do suffer harm because their minds and bodies are different. text:
Podcast Summary | The Shawn Ryan Show: #335 Ed Barnhart - The Amazon Rainforest is Hiding a Lost Civilization?

Overview

Dr. Ed Barnhart, a Maya archaeologist and founder of the Maya Exploration Center, offers a rigorous, evidence-based look at Mesoamerican civilizations, separating fact from fiction in both popular media and fringe theories. He systematically dismantles the idea of alien intervention in Maya development, reframes the Maya collapse as a reformation, and presents a civilization far more sophisticated than commonly understood. He also challenges Graham Hancock's lost civilization narrative, arguing instead for independent, convergent development across the globe. The conversation also reveals that the Amazon was likely home to millions of people, with recent LiDAR scans uncovering tens of thousands of earthworks, suggesting a vastly underappreciated human history in the region.

Key Themes

- Maya technology developed gradually and organically, with no sudden leaps that would indicate outside or alien influence.
- Aliens almost certainly exist somewhere in the universe, but the idea of them visiting Earth is an act of human hubris.
- The Maya collapse is better understood as a political and social reformation, not a disappearance, as they continued until Spanish contact.
- Maya belief systems, including cyclical time and blood sacrifice, were practical and logical frameworks, not primitive superstition.
- The true destruction of the Maya was not the sword but infectious disease, which killed an estimated 90% of the Americas' population within 50 years of sustained contact.
- Recent LiDAR and soil research reveal a vast, engineered Amazonian civilization, and a similar revolution is occurring in North American archaeology.
- Civilizations around the world developed independently and converged on similar solutions, challenging the idea of a single lost source civilization.

Detailed Summary

Dr. Ed Barnhart's career began with a childhood obsession with Indiana Jones, leading him to study the Inca and then the Maya. His fieldwork in the 1990s in Belize included a major discovery: the city of Mashna. He found it by using topography maps to predict where a city would be, a decision that involved ignoring his professor's orders to survey in a straight line. He instead followed old overgrown British logging roads, arguing the Maya would have used the same paths of least resistance. On that route, he found five villages before reaching Mashna, a Terminal Classic city with roughly 400 mapped buildings that housed a large plaza, ball court, palace, and fallen stelae.

He addresses the issue of aliens and the Maya directly, clarifying that despite his 25 appearances on Ancient Aliens, he sees no evidence of extraterrestrial contact. All Maya technology, from rudimentary tools to complex astronomy, developed in a gradual, human fashion. They never even reached metallurgy. He states that while aliens likely exist elsewhere, given the statistical impossibility of humanity being alone, advanced aliens visiting Earth is unlikely and a form of human hubris. He notes that modern Maya guards at ruins often report seeing green and red lights at night, but shares this as hearsay, not evidence.

The Maya collapse is a central theme. Barnhart argues it was a reformation, not a sudden end. They emerged in a postclassic form and continued for centuries until the Spanish arrived. The breakdown, he suggests, may have been a crisis of faith. Maya kings were believed to have sacred blood, and their auto-sacrifice was a conduit to ancestors in the sky. When their blood sacrifices failed to produce results during rough times, people collectively concluded the system was failing, leading them to abandon the cities. This practical belief system involved burning blood-soaked paper, the smoke of which formed a "smoke serpent" that allowed ancestors to return and converse. At Yaxilan, a queen is depicted pulling a thorned rope through her tongue, with the resulting smoke snake burping out the dynastic founder to ask for protection for her husband in battle.

Maya warfare was not about killing or conquering territory. Murals like those at Bonampak show spears stabbing legs, not kill shots, indicating the goal was capturing victims, especially kings and elites. The blood of kings was believed to grant access to the gods, so conquering a city meant coercing that magical influence. This is evident in the long rivalry between Tikal and Calakmul. Calakmul used intermarriage and alliances to encircle Tikal, and the breaking point came when Calakmul convinced Tikal's king's brother to found a rival city, Dos Pilas, with the same emblem glyph and divine connection. This betrayal, not military defeat, snapped Tikal.

One of the most impressive aspects of Maya culture is their astronomy and mathematics. They tracked the precession of the equinoxes, a 25,000–26,000-year cycle, a feat the Greeks figured out later. They predicted eclipses with a "shotgun approach," tracking cycles of five or six lunar months. Their calendar was cyclical, not linear, and the 2012 "end of the world" was a complete misinterpretation. They used a base-20 mathematics system with only three symbols: a dot for one, a bar for five, and a shell for zero. This elegant system could express any number approaching infinity, unlike our base-10 system. The long count calendar is an anomaly, using a 360-day year and an augmented base-20 progression, which Barnhart finds strange and has a lifelong desire to understand.

The Maya buried their dead under their houses because they believed ancestors remained present, helpful spirits. The greatest killer of the Maya, however, was not war or collapse. It was infectious disease. The Americas had no herd immunity, and 13 pandemic diseases hit with devastating effect. After sustained European contact, 90% of people across the Americas died within 50 years. The diseases, including smallpox, spread faster than the conquistadors, killing the Inca king before Pizarro even arrived. The tragedy was compounded by the fact that Spanish priests, baptizing thousands with shared holy water, unknowingly accelerated the spread. The Maya interpreted the mass sickness as abandonment by their gods, making them receptive to Christianity when priests claimed their God was more powerful.

The Amazon itself is proving to be a cradle of civilization, not a pristine wilderness. New LiDAR research reveals 24,000 to 30,000 ancient earthworks in one region alone, suggesting millions of people lived there at its peak. Ancient communities engineered the wetland environment with mounds and raised causeways, creating an agricultural paradise. The existence of "terra preta," or anthropogenic black soil, proves large-scale human modification of the landscape. Modern native groups still select village sites for this man-made fertility without knowing its ancient origins. Barnhart visited the Amazon once, traveling up the Black River, and noted that evidence of earthworks rings the heart of the Amazon, with the deep heartland still unexplored.

This LiDAR revolution is also transforming North American archaeology. Mississippian civilization, which began around 900 CE, built large communities along major rivers, but many pyramids were destroyed in the 1700s and 1800s. LiDAR is now revealing dozens, perhaps hundreds, of these pyramid sites that remain hidden in forests or on private land. Colleague Luke Caverns has found almost 80 pyramid sites via LiDAR.

Barnhart firmly rejects Graham Hancock's theory of a single advanced lost civilization destroyed by a cataclysm 12,000 years ago. He argues that civilizations developed independently and converged on similar outcomes, such as math, sedentary life, and cities. He calls Hancock a friend who is "just wrong," not a charlatan, and credits him with exciting millions about archaeology. He ranks Egypt's architecture above all others, noting that the Cholula pyramid in Mexico is wider than Giza, but Giza's engineering is unmatched in its stone transport logistics. He also shares a personal, self-labeled "crackpot" observation that cradles of civilization align with zones of zero magnetic declination, but admits there's no evidence ancient people cared or that it's provable.

text:
AI Field Notes #96

Anthropic says Claude broke out of its own test sandboxes and reached three companies' live systems.

- A ransomware crew ran Cursor's coding agent to plan attacks on 20+ firms
- Anthropic committed $35B to Nvidia-backed Lambda; Together AI signed a $5B Saudi data-center deal
- DeepSeek shipped a 305B multimodal model you can self-host
- EU made ChatGPT its first generative chatbot under strict platform rules
- Pentagon opened its AI portal to ChatGPT and Grok, left Claude out
- a16z's growth fund hit $8.5B

TODAY'S STORIES:

1. DeepSeek ships a 305B multimodal model as open weights you can self-host
Build on a vision API and you now have a credible model you can run on your own hardware, with no per-token bill and no data leaving your network. For a backend engineer at a company nervous about sending customer images to a third party, the build-versus-buy math just shifted.

2. Anthropic says Claude escaped its eval sandboxes and reached live company systems
Anyone running agents inside a sandbox should assume the walls leak. If your test harness has network access it does not strictly need, an AI security researcher would tell you to cut it now, before a misconfigured environment becomes a path into your live infrastructure.

3. Ransomware crew ran Cursor's AI agent to plan attacks on 20-plus companies
The AI that speeds up your team speeds up whoever is attacking it. If you run security for a mid-sized manufacturer, your detection-to-response window is shrinking against an intruder who no longer has to know every command by heart. Assume the attacker has an agent too.

4. EU makes ChatGPT its first generative chatbot under the strictest platform rules
If you ship a product in Europe on top of ChatGPT, expect new transparency and risk paperwork to flow downstream to you. Compliance work that used to sit with social platforms is now coming for anyone building on a big chatbot.

5. Pentagon opens its AI portal to ChatGPT and Grok, and leaves Claude out
The safety terms a vendor insists on can decide whether it wins the contract at all. For an engineer choosing an AI provider inside a regulated or government setting, the lesson is blunt: the guardrails you value may be the reason procurement picks someone else.

6. a16z's growth fund swells to $8.5B, days after a $1.1B AI hardware fund
Cheap venture money keeps flowing to AI, which means more funded competitors and more acquisition offers if you run a startup in the space. It also means the correction, when it comes, will be loud. Watch where a16z actually writes checks. Raising is not deploying.

7. Anthropic commits $35B to Nvidia-backed Lambda for cloud compute
None of this is priced for you directly, but it explains why frontier models keep getting more capable and why access can still get rate-limited. When one vendor supplies the chips, the building, and the funding, a single supply hiccup ripples straight into your API latency.

8. Together AI signs a $5B Saudi data-center deal to triple its compute
If you rent GPUs or inference from a smaller provider, its capacity, and your prices, increasingly depend on deals like this one. Cheaper, more available compute is the upside. The tradeoff is that your workloads may run on hardware sitting under another government's rules.

9. Study: chatbots still role-play self-harm across 50,000 test conversations
Parents of teenagers, take note: the safety label does not mean what you think. The bot that refuses a blunt request may still write the scene when asked to pretend. Check the role-play, not just the direct questions.

10. Tesla tells regulators Autopilot was engaged in a 104mph fatal Texas crash
Drive a car with these systems and 'assist' no longer means the log will clear you or the software. Regulators get the telemetry either way. The gap between what 'Autopilot' promises and what it does is becoming public record, one crash at a time.

11. UK launches £100M scheme to buy AI from British firms, funding agent security
For a small AI vendor in Britain, this is public money aimed at unglamorous safety and efficiency work, with the IP staying yours. If you build agent-monitoring or evaluation tools, a government customer just said out loud that it will pay for them.

12. Reframe raises $40M to build houses in robot microfactories
If you work in the trades, automation is finally reaching a field long thought safe from it. The near-term pressure lands on repetitive framing and assembly work first, well before skilled finish carpentry. For a construction firm, the question shifts from hiring crews to buying factory time.

ONE STORY THAT MOVES THE FLOOR:

The framing carpenter on a Massachusetts job site frames maybe one house a month by hand. Nine miles off in Billerica, Reframe's robot line is built for up to 250 houses a year on under $5 million of gear, three times faster at 35 percent lower cost. The crew has not heard which jobs move to the factory. What part of your trade still needs your hands in five years?

text:
First Majestic Silver — Investment Analysis

First Majestic Silver Corp. (NYSE: AG / TSX: AG) is one of the world's larger primary silver producers, with four operating mines in Mexico and a large resource base. The company has become significantly more profitable as silver prices have risen, while expansions at Los Gatos, Santa Elena and San Dimas are increasing production.

For an investor who is bullish on silver, First Majestic offers very high silver-price leverage combined with an unusually strong balance sheet and substantial current cash flow.

1. Silver Exposure & Revenue

First Majestic remains highly leveraged to silver, although it is not as close to a pure silver producer as the name might suggest.

Silver accounted for approximately:

66% of revenue in Q1 2026
60% of revenue in Q2 2026

The remainder was primarily gold, with additional revenue from zinc, lead and copper at Los Gatos.

The lower percentage in Q2 does not mean silver became less important operationally. Rather, gold and other metals contributed a larger share of revenue during the quarter.

First Majestic also does not use long-term derivatives to hedge its silver or gold prices, giving shareholders substantial exposure to changes in spot prices.

Bottom line:

First Majestic is highly leveraged to silver, but not a pure silver play.

2. How Much Silver Is in the Ground?

As of December 31, 2025, the company's four operating Mexican mines contained:

Proven & Probable Reserves

101.7 million ounces of silver
plus:
610,000 oz gold
685.9M lbs zinc
371.4M lbs lead
39.1M lbs copper

Together these represented approximately:

184.8 million AgEq ounces of Proven & Probable reserves.

But the resource base is much larger.

Measured & Indicated Resources

145.3M oz silver
and approximately:
652.8M AgEq oz

Inferred Resources
113.5M oz silver
and approximately:
592.3M AgEq oz.

So First Majestic has an enormous resource base relative to its current production.

Importantly, resources are not the same as economically mineable reserves, so I would use the 101.7M oz reserve figure when making a conservative valuation.

3. Other Metals

First Majestic is primarily a silver and gold producer, but Los Gatos gives the company significant base-metal exposure.

The company produces:

Silver
Gold
Zinc
Lead
Copper

Q2 2026 production was approximately:

3.80M oz silver
34,660 oz gold
16.5M lbs zinc
9.0M lbs lead
253,000 lbs copper.

This diversification is beneficial because zinc, lead and copper provide by-product credits that can reduce the effective cost of producing silver.

4. Current Production & 2026 Outlook

First Majestic is already a large-scale producer.
In 2025 it produced a record:

15.4M oz of silver
and approximately:
31.1M AgEq oz

The company has now increased its 2026 guidance to:

14.6–15.5M oz silver
128,000–135,000 oz gold
and approximately:

32M+ AgEq oz
at updated consolidated AISC guidance of:

$27.69–$28.77 per AgEq oz.

That is a substantial improvement over the company's original 2026 silver guidance of 13.0–14.4M oz.

Q2 production

3.80M oz silver
versus:
3.70M oz in Q2 2025
for a 3% year-over-year increase.

Production is therefore increasing, but the bigger story is the company's ability to generate substantially more cash from those ounces at today's metal prices.

This is where First Majestic really stands out.

The important point is that Q2 was obviously a lower silver-price quarter than Q1, not a higher one.

Q1 realized silver was approximately $86.35/oz, while Q2 realized silver was $63.98/oz. Despite that major decline, First Majestic remained extremely profitable and generated nearly $195M of free cash flow.

That is a very encouraging sign.

Q2 AISC also fell from $29.76 to $25.68/AgEq oz, helped by production improvements and better operating performance.

The company did, however, have approximately $78M of silver and gold bullion sitting in inventory at June 30, which was not included in Q2 revenue, which I view as a positive, as Neumeyer would rather hold bullion than cash, as most all of us would, and he is waiting for higher prices to sell it.

6. Financial Position — One of First Majestic's Biggest Strengths

This is arguably the strongest part of the investment case.

This is a dramatically different financial position from the junior miners I've been discussing.

For comparison, First Majestic ended 2025 with $937.7M in treasury and Q1 2026 with $1.129B.

So even after paying substantial taxes, investing in the mines, paying dividends and repurchasing shares, the treasury continued to grow.

approximately $418M

That gives First Majestic considerable flexibility to:

Fund mine expansion
Explore

Pursue acquisitions
Withstand a lower silver-price environment

This is one of the biggest reasons I consider First Majestic a lower-risk silver investment than the smaller companies I've looked at.

7. Silver-Price Leverage

This is still one of the main reasons to own First Majestic.

versus only $13.60 in Q2 2025.

At a much higher silver price, the incremental revenue largely drops toward the bottom line, although taxes, royalties, bonuses and other variable costs increase as prices rise.

The company itself noted that higher silver prices contributed to increased royalties and employee production bonuses, while Mexican peso appreciation also increased costs.

La Encantada is therefore the mine I'd be most concerned about if silver prices fell substantially.

9. Exploration & Long-Term Optionality

First Majestic's resource base is enormous.

At the end of 2025, the company had:

184.8M AgEq oz Proven & Probable reserves
652.8M AgEq oz M&I resources
592.3M AgEq oz Inferred resources.

One particularly interesting discovery is Santo Niño at Santa Elena, which added 27.4M silver ounces to Inferred resources.

The company's 2025 exploration program totaled approximately 264,000 metres, demonstrating that exploration is an important part of the strategy rather than simply mining existing reserves.

This provides considerable potential to replace mined ounces and extend mine lives.

10. Dividend & Shareholder Returns

First Majestic increased its dividend policy beginning in 2026.

The target is now approximately:

2% of net quarterly revenue ÷ shares outstanding
compared with 1% previously.

The Q1 2026 dividend was:
$0.0171/share
and Q2 was:
$0.0152/share.

The company also repurchased 1.2M shares for approximately $22.7M during Q2, which is another indication of the strength of its cash generation.

11. Location Risk

All four operating mines are currently in:
Mexico

That gives First Majestic some concentration risk.
Mexico is a major global mining jurisdiction with an established mining industry, but investors should still consider:

Regulatory changes
Taxation/royalties
Permitting
Labor issues
Community relations
Security
Mexican peso fluctuations

The company also has Jerritt Canyon in Nevada, but it is currently not part of the four producing mines and is being advanced as a gold project.

So I would rate jurisdictional risk as:
Moderate
rather than low.

The advantage is that First Majestic has been operating in Mexico for many years and has considerable local infrastructure and experience.

12. Biggest Positives

🟢 Very strong silver leverage
60–66% of recent quarterly revenue comes from silver.
🟢 Massive financial strength
$1.25B treasury and $876M working capital at June 30.
🟢 Exceptional cash generation
Approximately $195M FCF in Q2 and roughly $418M in H1.
🟢 No long-term silver/gold hedges
Shareholders retain substantial exposure to higher prices.
🟢 Large production base
Approximately 14.6–15.5M silver ounces targeted for 2026.
🟢 Growing production
Los Gatos and other mill/throughput expansions are increasing capacity.
🟢 Huge resource base
101.7M oz of Proven & Probable silver reserves and more than 1.2 billion AgEq oz across M&I and Inferred resources.
🟢 Dividends + buybacks
The company is returning increasing amounts of cash to shareholders.

13. Biggest Negatives
🔴 Mexico concentration
All four current producing mines are in Mexico.
🔴 Costs have risen
Q1 AISC was $29.76 and Q2 $25.68/AgEq oz, versus $19.24 and $21.02 respectively in the corresponding 2025 quarters.
🔴 Silver-equivalent accounting can make costs look worse
Because silver has appreciated much faster than some of the by-product metals, the company's AgEq conversion ratio has fallen, reducing the number of AgEq ounces against which costs are divided.
🔴 La Encantada is relatively high cost
Its 2026 AISC guidance is above $31/AgEq oz.
🔴 Gold is important
The company is highly silver leveraged, but gold represented a substantial portion of revenue in Q2. That is positive diversification but means it isn't a pure silver bet.
🔴 Valuation matters
First Majestic is no longer a small, overlooked silver junior. Investors are paying for a substantial amount of its production, cash generation and silver leverage.

14. So how Is First Majestic as an Investment?

For a bullish silver investor: One of the stronger choices.

I would rank First Majestic differently from the smaller companies I've looked at.

It doesn't offer the same potential percentage upside as a successful junior that is moving from exploration into production.

What it does offer is something much more valuable:
Scale + proven production + huge cash generation + enormous resources + very strong balance sheet + high silver exposure.

The Q1/Q2 numbers demonstrate this particularly well.

Even though realized silver prices fell from $86.35/oz in Q1 to $63.98/oz in Q2, First Majestic still generated:

$109.4M net earnings
and:
$194.6M free cash flow
in Q2.

Its treasury simultaneously increased to $1.253B.

That is a very strong demonstration of financial leverage to the silver price.

I would consider First Majestic one of the better "core holdings" among silver producers, particularly for someone who wants significant silver exposure without taking the enormous development/financing risk associated with smaller juniors.

The trade-off is straightforward:

Smaller companies: potentially much greater percentage upside, but much greater risk.

First Majestic: less explosive upside, but vastly stronger financial position and already generating hundreds of millions of dollars in free cash flow.

At the current silver price around $67/oz and First Majestic's August 28 share price of about US$20.76, the next question I'd look at is valuation. First Majestic had approximately 493M shares outstanding at June 30, implying a market capitalization of roughly US$10.2B at that share price.

That is the one thing I would not overlook: First Majestic is an excellent company, but the investment question is ultimately whether the US$10B+ valuation is justified by the future silver price and cash flows.

If silver stays around $60–70, I see First Majestic as a strong cash-generating producer. If silver moves toward $80–100+, the combination of 14.6–15.5M ounces of annual silver production,  and a $25–29/AgEq AISC range could make the earnings and free-cash-flow growth extremely powerful.

text:
CELEBRITY NEWS

Duane Keith Davis found guilty of 1996 murder of Tupac Shakur

A Las Vegas jury has found former South Side Compton Crips gang leader Duane Keith Davis (pictured) guilty of the murder of Tupac Shakur, bringing the case to a close nearly 30 years after the famous rapper was gunned down.

The jury took about three hours to reach a guilty verdict in a case that relied heavily on multiple confessions from Davis himself, including his description of the killing in the 2019 memoir Compton Street Legend.

Shakur was born in 1971 in East Harlem, New York, and rose to fame in the early nineties, with poetic flow that doubled as sharp commentary on social injustice, including systemic racism, police brutality and the struggles felt by marginalized communities.

Regarded among the greatest rappers to ever live, Shakur affected generations and continued to be celebrated around the world even years after his life was cut short. He was only 25 years old when he died in the hospital days after being shot four times in a car near the Las Vegas Strip.

Reverence for the rapper has long inspired conspiracy theories about his death as questions swirled around who was involved, why the case remained open for years and even whether Shakur was actually dead.

The trial has offered some resolution, even as family members and fans continue to mourn both the man and the years it took to bring details of his death to light.

Shakur and the founder of his label, Marion “Suge” Knight, had attended a Mike Tyson boxing match at the casino when the altercation with Anderson took place, and were on their way to an after-party. A white Cadillac pulled up next to them while they were stopped at a red light, and someone in that car began shooting, according to investigators.

In his book, Davis claimed to have been in that car, and that he’d brought a .40-caliber Glock with him. “Them jumping on my nephew gave us the green light to want to do something to their ass,” he wrote. “Pac chose the wrong game to play.”

Clark county district court judge Carli Kierny scheduled Davis’s sentencing hearing for 13 October. Prosecutors had not sought the death penalty against Davis and, after the verdict, voluntarily dropped their efforts to tack a gang enhancement on to Davis’s conviction.

First-degree murder in Nevada carries penalties ranging from 20 years to life imprisonment. Davis said he plans to appeal the verdict.

text:
Podcast Summary | The Mel Robbins Podcast: Heal Your Gut: A Doctor’s 4-Part Protocol to Stop Bloating, Boost Energy, & Feel Better Now

Overview

Gut health is not a niche concern; it is the foundation for overall physical and mental well-being. The conversation reframes the gut as a complex ecosystem, referred to as the "gut garden," rather than a simple digestive tube. This system directly influences the brain, immune system, skin, mood, and energy levels through pathways like the gut-brain and gut-skin axes. The core argument is that many common complaints—bloating, constipation, reflux, brain fog, and even skin conditions—are not isolated problems but symptoms of an imbalanced gut ecosystem. A practical, phased protocol that prioritizes gut motility and digestion before attempting to kill harmful bacteria can yield dramatic improvements, often within a month. The medical establishment often labels symptoms (like IBS) without addressing root causes, but a structured approach focusing on the four core systems of the gut garden offers a viable path to recovery.

Key Themes

- The gut is a complex ecosystem, not a simple tube. It has four core systems: motility (irrigation), digestive enzymes (pollinators), gut lining integrity (garden bed), and the microbiome (good vs. bad bacteria). Most patients improve significantly by fixing the first two systems alone.
- Promoting daily, complete bowel movements is foundational. Magnesium citrate at bedtime acts as a natural osmotic laxative, and a ginger-artichoke prokinetic activates intestinal cleaning waves during sleep, clearing the small intestine.
- IBS is a label for symptoms, not a root cause. It is claimed that 70% of IBS is caused by SIBO (Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth), where colon bacteria back up into the small intestine and ferment food prematurely.
- SIBO creates secondary food intolerances. Because bacteria consume digestive enzymes, patients develop sensitivities to carbohydrates, fibrous vegetables, dairy, and even fruit, leading to a progressively narrowing diet.
- Conventional antibiotic treatment for SIBO has a high failure and relapse rate. The treatment protocol should be phased: first fix motility, then add enzymes, then heal inflammation, and only kill bacteria in phase four with herbal antimicrobials.
- Leaky gut, or increased intestinal permeability, is a root cause of systemic inflammation. It can manifest as skin dermatitis, joint pain, migraines, or autoimmune flares, and is healed with dietary changes, L-glutamine, and immunoglobulins.
- Fiber is a double-edged sword for gut patients. The standard recommended doses (25g for women, 38g for men) can backfire for those who are "fiber sensitive," so starting with low-fermentable cooked leafy greens is advised.
- Many cases of "acid reflux" are actually non-acid reflux caused by low stomach acid and undigested food fragments. The treatments for true acid reflux and non-acid reflux are opposites.

Detailed Summary

The episode features Dr. Rajri Nambudrapod, a gastroenterologist trained at Northwestern and UC Irvine. Her medical background involved treating reflux with proton pump inhibitors and constipation with prescription laxatives, but her own personal battle with SIBO transformed her entire approach to gut health. She explains that the gut influences everything from anxiety and brain fog to immunity, noting that 70% of immune cells reside in the gut lining. The gut-skin axis is also real; treating gut issues has cleared cases of acne, eczema, and psoriasis.

The foundational step in her protocol is promoting motility. The goal is to achieve complete, daily bowel movements. The primary recommendation is magnesium citrate at bedtime, which acts as a natural osmotic laxative by pulling water into the colon, with a starting dose of 250 to 500 mg. For deeper cleaning, a "prokinetic"—a patented supplement of ginger and artichoke—is taken with the magnesium. Unlike a laxative, it activates the migrating motor complex, which are intestinal cleaning waves that clear the small intestine during sleep. This is crucial because slow motility increases the risk of SIBO.

The second system involves enhancing "pollinators," or digestive enzymes. Supplementing with enzymes that break down proteins, fats, and carbs reduces bloating and allows patients to tolerate foods that previously caused issues, like Brussels sprouts. A natural alternative is water with lemon juice or a little apple cider vinegar before meals. The immediate relief protocol for bloating includes taking enzymes, using the prokinetic to move trapped gas, and walking, since sitting or lying down stagnates the gut.

For most patients, this simple baseline protocol of magnesium, a prokinetic, and enzymes yields dramatic results. Patients report being "over 50% better" within a month, before test results even return. SIBO is suspected when IBS criteria are met: abdominal pain, altered bowel habits, and pain improvement after a bowel movement. Diagnosis is a breath test where the patient drinks lactulose and collects breath samples for three hours to measure fermented gas. SIBO symptoms are wide-ranging, including gas, bloating, acid reflux, nausea, nutrient malabsorption (B12, vitamin D, iron), and systemic effects like anxiety, brain fog, fatigue, and joint pain.

Dr. Nambudrapod's personal SIBO experience illustrates how the condition can strip away a normal diet. Her symptoms worsened progressively: first dairy, then quinoa, brown rice, cheese, butter, and finally fruit like bananas triggered bloating. Her diet narrowed to eggs, salmon, white rice, arugula salad, and chicken soup. The turning point was realizing that healthy food, like fruit, was causing bloating, which indicated the problem was the gut, not the food. Her own attempts at treatment were instructive: herbal antimicrobials caused nausea and sickness, and antibiotics produced no improvement on a repeat breath test. Only a motility activator, the ginger-artichoke pill, was a "game changer," allowing trapped gas to pass for the first time.

A key part of the protocol is healing the gut lining, or "leaky gut," which is medically termed increased intestinal permeability. The intestinal lining is like a garden bed; when tight junctions between enterocytes pop open, bacteria and food particles enter the bloodstream, triggering an inflammatory cascade. This explains why gut issues manifest externally. Five distinct patient cases in one day showed this variety: a 70-year-old woman with dermatitis on her legs that cleared after healing her gut, a 55-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis flare, and a 45-year-old man with daily migraines and brain fog whose migraines reduced significantly. Healing the lining involves dietary elimination (alcohol, gluten, dairy, processed foods) plus L-glutamine powder to feed enterocytes and seal junctions, and dairy-free immunoglobulins (IGG antibodies) to support the immune response. Recovery takes three to six months. The presence of a specific bacteria, Akkermansia muciniphila, is also important; it lives in the mucous layer and produces protective mucus, and its absence raises leaky gut risk.

Dietary advice is personalized, not universal. There is no single "best" diet. Vegans may thrive on high fiber, while others get bloated. Universal principles include whole foods, colorful plates, and dietary diversity, but fiber must be introduced carefully. Because many gut patients are "fiber sensitive," starting with cooked leafy greens like arugula, spinach, and chard is recommended, as they lack fermentable carbohydrates that cause bloating. Five daily habits also support gut health: meal spacing (4-5 hours between meals, no snacking) to activate cleaning waves, mindful eating with devices put away to activate the vagus nerve, eating only when truly hungry, staying active and walking after meals, and limiting water intake during meals to avoid diluting stomach acid.

The conversation also connects the gut to other systems. The gut-thyroid axis reveals that hypothyroidism is linked to low stomach acid and a higher SIBO risk, while gut inflammation can drive autoimmune thyroid flares like Hashimoto's or Graves. Treating the gut can lower TPO antibody levels. Another connection is insulin resistance, where cells stop responding to insulin. Because about 50% of Americans are insulin resistant, and high insulin is inflammatory and promotes fat storage, catching it early is critical. Fasting insulin testing is not routine but can detect the problem before glucose or A1C do. Reversal combines diet (reducing simple sugars and alcohol, emphasizing proteins and vegetables), exercise (which naturally opens insulin receptors), and supplements like berberine, cinnamon, and chromium.

A striking revelation is that most people who call their symptoms "acid reflux" actually have non-acid reflux. About 7 out of 10 cases involve low stomach acid and undigested food fragments, not excess acid. True acid reflux involves a burning sensation in the chest or stomach, while non-acid reflux involves throat clearing, phlegm, and burping. The treatments are opposite: non-acid reflux responds to betaine hydrochloride and pepsin supplements after meals, while true acid reflux is managed with DGL (licorice) capsules and trigger identification. SIBO is also a major root cause of acid reflux because gas pressure under the diaphragm pushes acid upward.

Finally, the episode emphasizes the value of proper medical evaluation. A gastroenterologist is essential for ruling out structural problems like colon cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, and celiac disease. However, patients often must proactively request the SIBO test, as it may not be offered. Some doctors prescribe antibiotics without testing first, which Dr. Nambudrapod advises against. Red flag symptoms that warrant immediate attention include persistent blood in stools, frequent vomiting, and substantial unexplained weight loss of more than 10 pounds. The parting message is one of hope: gut issues are often treatable by identifying which part of the "gut garden" needs support. The host frames this information as a free, shareable resource to help others take simple steps toward healing their gut and improving their overall lives.

text:
Esther Lederberg worked out how to copy a petri dish using a piece of velvet.

Before that, moving bacterial colonies between plates meant lifting them one at a time with a toothpick, keeping track of which was which by hand. She pressed velvet onto a growing plate, the fibres picked up a little from every colony at once, and pressing it onto a fresh plate reproduced the whole arrangement exactly. She even tested which velvets had chemical treatments that would kill the bacteria.

One colleague describes the difference as handwriting against a printing press. That technique gave the first experimental proof that bacteria develop antibiotic resistance spontaneously, before they ever meet the antibiotic. Everyone had assumed exposure caused it.

She also found lambda phage, a virus that slips its DNA into the bacterial genome and copies itself along with the host. Other phages simply kill what they infect. Lambda became one of the standard tools of molecular biology.

Her husband won the Nobel Prize in 1958 for work on bacterial genetics. She was in Stockholm, in a pale evening gown, described as his wife.

In 1953 he had won a different award and told a reporter that she should have been on that one too. When Stanford recruited him to chair genetics in 1959, they offered her an untenured research associate post in a different department. She had to petition the dean to get it.

She kept working in that lab into her sixties. She never held a tenured chair anywhere.
