Wrongfully Deactivated? Here's Exactly What To Do Before It's Too Late
— By Sergio Avedian —
For most Uber and Lyft drivers, there isn't a bigger fear than opening the app and seeing one message: "Your account has been deactivated."
No warning. No explanation. No opportunity to tell your side of the story.
For many drivers, rideshare isn't just a side hustle.  It's how they pay their mortgage, buy groceries, or support their  families. A sudden deactivation can cut off that income overnight.
While  Uber and Lyft have every right to remove drivers who violate their  terms of service or create safety concerns, I've also spoken with  countless drivers who believe they were deactivated unfairly after a false passenger complaint, an identity verification issue, or what appeared to be an automated decision.
The good news is that you aren't powerless. If your account is ever deactivated, here's exactly what you should do.
1. Start Saving Evidence Before You Ever Need It

The biggest mistake drivers make is waiting until after they're deactivated to gather evidence.

By  then, it's often too late. Think of yourself as the owner of a small  business. Every ride is a business transaction, and good businesses keep  records.

Some of the most valuable evidence includes:

Screenshots of trip requests and earnings

Messages between you and passengers

Weekly earnings statements
Trip receipts

GPS records

Maintenance records

Vehicle inspection reports

Insurance documents

If  something unusual happens during a trip, make notes while it's still  fresh in your mind. Small details that seem unimportant today could  become critical later.

Make sure you subscribe to our YouTube Channel for new Show Me The Money Club videos every week, plus all the latest  chatter, insights, and news from the delivery and rideshare industries.

2. A Dashcam Is One of the Best Investments You Can Make

If you drive professionally, a dashcam isn't a luxury anymore. It's business insurance.

I've  seen numerous situations where dashcam footage completely changed the  outcome of a complaint. Whether it's a passenger claiming reckless  driving, inappropriate behavior, or damage that never occurred, video  evidence removes much of the uncertainty.

Ideally,  use a camera that records both the road ahead and the vehicle's  interior, where permitted by local law. Make sure passengers are  notified if your state requires consent for audio recording. Hopefully  you'll never need the footage.

But if you do, you'll be glad you have it.

3. Don't Panic When You Receive a Deactivation Notice

Your  first reaction might be frustration or anger. That's understandable.  But sending an emotional email or arguing with customer support rarely  helps your case.
Instead, carefully read the reason provided for the deactivation. Sometimes  accounts are temporarily suspended because of missing documents, failed  identity verification, or routine background check reviews.

If  the issue involves a passenger complaint, respond professionally and  stick to the facts. Avoid making accusations or attacking the passenger.

The goal is to demonstrate that you're cooperative, credible, and willing to provide evidence.

4. Build a Strong Appeal

A successful appeal is based on facts not emotions.
Include:

A clear timeline of events

Relevant screenshots

Dashcam footage if available

Witness statements if applicable
Any documentation that contradicts the complaint

Keep  your explanation organized and concise. Support agents review countless  cases every day. The easier you make it for them to understand your  position, the better.

If  your appeal is denied, don't necessarily stop there. Politely request  another review if you believe important information was overlooked.

5. Understand Arbitration

Many  drivers don't realize that when they signed up for Uber or Lyft, they  agreed to dispute resolution procedures that often include arbitration  instead of traditional lawsuits. Small claims court is another way to  deal with deactivations.

Arbitration  isn't appropriate for every case, but if your deactivation caused  significant financial harm and you believe it violated your rights or  the company's own policies, it may be worth understanding your legal options.

Review your driver agreement carefully so you know what rights and deadlines apply.

6. Know When It's Time to Contact an Attorney

Not every deactivation requires legal representation. However, you should consider speaking with an attorney if:

You believe you were discriminated against.
Your account was deactivated after reporting safety concerns or illegal conduct.

The company failed to follow its own procedures.

You suffered substantial financial damages.

Your appeals have been exhausted and strong evidence supports your case.
Many  attorneys who handle employment and gig economy cases offer an initial  consultation, allowing you to better understand your options before  deciding how to proceed.

The latest episode of The Rideshare Guy Podcast is LIVE! Check out RSG269: This $12K EV Could Change Uber Driving Forever With Bingo Tech

Don't Put All Your Income on One Platform

This may be the most important lesson of all.

Even  if you've never had a problem with Uber or Lyft, remember that neither  company guarantees permanent access to its platform. That's why I  encourage drivers to diversify.

Sign up for multiple rideshare and delivery apps.  Keep your documents current across every platform. If one account is  temporarily suspended, having alternatives can keep money coming in  while you resolve the issue.

Treat your gig work like an investment portfolio. Diversification isn't just smart for investors; it's smart for drivers too.

My Final Take

Nobody wants to think about being deactivated, but every professional driver should have a plan before it happens.
Protect  yourself with documentation. Invest in a quality dashcam. Stay  professional during the appeals process. Understand your rights,  including arbitration, and don't hesitate to seek legal advice when the  situation warrants it.

Most  importantly, remember that preparation is your best defense. You can't  control every passenger complaint or every automated decision made by Uber or Lyft. But you can control how well prepared you are if your account is ever put at risk.

In today's rideshare industry, protecting your account is just as important as earning your next fare.

Be safe out there!

text:
Dear friends,

As summer gives way to September and the final four months of 2026 come into view, I want to speak to you from the heart.

As much as a human being can love an institution, I love the Catholic Church and the United States of America.

I love them the way you love a family: without illusions, fully aware of their failures, stubborn about their promise, and unwilling to abandon them to their worst impulses.

Both are blessed. Both are broken. Both are capable of greatness. And both are worth fighting for.

That is what Letters from Leo exists to do.

This project is an act of service to a Church and a country I believe can be better. It is a refusal to let cynicism, despair, or numbness have the final word.

Our mission is simple and demanding: to make America more just, less cold, and brimming with hope.

That means standing up to the defining threats of our age — creeping authoritarianism and a tech-industrial oligarchy that treats human beings as data points and democracy as a friction problem.

We intend to meet this moment the way serious people always have: by learning from the past, studying what is unfolding now, and using that truth to guide what we build next.

This is not just a newsletter. It is a project born at a McDonald’s off St. Peter’s Square that has become a movement — a growing community of people of all faiths and no faith, drawn together by the witness of Pope Leo XIV and the moral clarity he is bringing into the public square.

You have watched that witness all year. On America’s 250th birthday, we were on Lampedusa as Leo stood with the island’s migrants, and in Magnifica Humanitas he gave the Church its charter for defending human dignity in the age of artificial intelligence.

Inspired by that witness, we are trying to spark what Leo and Francis have called a “revolution of tenderness” in American politics, culture, and media.

I have a dogmatic belief you and I are living through a providential moment.

Just as God raised up a pope from behind the Iron Curtain to help defeat communism, God has raised up a pope from the Americas to defeat authoritarianism — and to call our nation back to a land of dreams and dignity for all who inhabit it.

That providence now asks something of us. On November 3, sixty-three days from now, Americans will vote in the first nationwide election of Leo’s pontificate, and the final four months of 2026 will decide whether the cruelty running our government receives a mandate or a rebuke.

I dedicate my entire heart to ensuring we make America more just, less cold, and more alive with hope.

To paraphrase Peter: I bring neither silver nor gold to this project. I bring the greatest gifts I’ve received — my back, my mind, my heart, and my faith. I offer them in the belief that you and I were made for this moment — to be repairers of the breach.

Letters from Leo is sustained entirely by readers like you. There are no corporate sponsors. No billionaire benefactors. Just ordinary people choosing to invest in something they believe matters.

If you feel the same energy I do, the same urgency I do, the same passion I do, and the same hopefulness I do, I’m asking for your help in three concrete ways:

Subscribe as a paid member to receive exclusive posts about the life and formation of Pope Leo and help sustain this newsletter.

Donate with a one-time gift to fuel this project’s mission.

Share this post (and Letters from Leo) with a friend who might enjoy it.

And if you are someone who prays, I humbly ask for your prayers — for me, for this work, and for Pope Leo, who carries a very heavy cross.

Thank you for being here. Thank you for believing that this country can still be made more just, more humane, and more worthy of our love.

Let us rise, you and I, and make of this blessed but broken nation something more blessed still.

It’s time to get to work. I’ll see you on the road.

Christopher https://t.co/HmqlIMYVmT

text:
A lot of people warned me that Utah has become incredibly expensive, especially when it comes to housing. I don’t doubt them at all—locals are obviously facing genuine pressure as prices continue to rise.

However, as someone living in Sydney, Australia, I became curious about what “expensive” looks like compared with the housing market I already know. Salt Lake City seemed like the closest comparison to Sydney within Utah, so I did some research and created this graphic.

The difference genuinely surprised me.

A median detached house in Sydney costs around A$1.734 million, compared with approximately A$945,000 in Salt Lake City. An apartment or condo costs around A$849,000 in Sydney, compared with approximately A$509,000 in Salt Lake City.

I’m aware that Salt Lake City is much smaller than Sydney and that prices can vary considerably across Utah. I also understand that local wages, mortgage rates, property taxes, healthcare, insurance and HOA fees all affect whether a home is genuinely affordable. I’m certainly not suggesting Utah is cheap or dismissing the difficulties local families are experiencing.

It simply shows how much our idea of “expensive” can depend on where we’re coming from. By Sydney standards, Salt Lake City still appears to offer considerably more house and land for the money.

For those who live in Utah, does this comparison reflect what you’re seeing on the ground?

text:
ISHARES ETHEREUM TRUST $ETHA HOLDS $8.5B OF ETHER. THE VERSION THAT PAYS IS A DIFFERENT FUND:

iShares Ethereum Trust ETHA at $18.57 (after hours), -$0.15 / -0.80% from today's close. It finished regular trading at $18.72, +$0.35 / +1.91%. BlackRock's fund has one job: buy real ether, store it, and cut the pile into shares that trade in a brokerage account like a stock. Spot means it holds the actual coin rather than a contract about one - $8.54B of it.

The bottom line: ether pays a small income to people who help run its network, and bitcoin has nothing like that. This fund passes that income to nobody. BlackRock runs a second one that does. August is the month the difference stopped being a footnote.

WHERE THE TWO BIGGEST COINS SIT

Bitcoin, ticker BTC: $78,317, +0.72% over the last 24 hours. Ethereum, ticker ETH, the second-largest digital asset: $2,460, +1.88% across the same window. Ether moved about two and a half times as far, and that is the month in miniature. Across August this fund gained $4.65 / +33.0%. iShares Bitcoin Trust at $44.33 (after hours), -$0.34 / -0.76% from today's $44.67 close, itself +$0.77 / +1.75% today, gained $9.03 / +25.3% over the same four weeks.

Nearly eight points of daylight between the two largest coins in one month.

THE THING ETHER DOES THAT BITCOIN CANNOT

Ether owners can lock their coins up to help check and record transactions on the network, and the network pays them for the work - currently around 2.7% a year. That is staking, and roughly 34% of all the ether in existence is now doing it, against about 29% in January. Bitcoin offers no equivalent. Holding it pays zero, always, by design.

TWO FUNDS, ONE COIN, ONE PAYMENT

This fund does not stake. It holds ether in cold storage and charges 0.25% a year, collected by selling coin out of the fund, so each share stands on very slightly less ether over time. Nothing is ever distributed.

iShares Staked Ethereum Trust closed at $31.96, +$0.60 / +1.91% today. Launched March 12, 2026, it stakes 70% to 95% of its ether through Coinbase Prime validators and hands 82% of the gross rewards to shareholders monthly, BlackRock keeping 18%. It paid $0.03 a share on August 11 - about $0.36 a year at that pace, near 1.1% of the share price.

The honest half: the fund that pays holds $863.3M, the fund that pays nothing holds $8.54B. Nearly ten dollars have gone into the silent one for every dollar in the one that distributes.

Neither can be a Len5 name, and that is structural rather than a judgment. Every Len5 weighs a business, and a vault with a fee attached has no earnings and no growth rate. Even the staking fund fails the Income Len5, which wants cash a business genuinely funds; here it comes from a network.

WHERE THE MONEY WENT

Since August 17, US spot ether funds have taken in about $1.42B across nine trading days without one day of net selling, per Farside Investors. This fund took $1.02B of it, 72 cents in every dollar.

The scale makes it land. In the week to August 28, US spot bitcoin funds pulled in $924.5M and spot ether funds about $824M - nearly the same money into a category a fraction of the size, since BlackRock's bitcoin fund holds $61.35B against this one's $8.54B, roughly seven to one.

THE TWO COMPANIES IN THIS

- Strategy, the company formerly called MicroStrategy, at $130.62 (after hours), -$2.32 / -1.75% from today's $132.94 close, +$5.63 / +4.42% on the day. The Tysons Corner, Virginia company holds bitcoin and raises money to hold more; today it said it added 4,603 coins between August 24 and 30 for $369.7M, taking the pile to 845,050. It has paid $63.73B for them, $75,412 a coin against $78,317 tonight - the largest corporate bitcoin owner on earth is ahead about 3.9% on the whole position, and owns no ether at all. It is on no Len5: the $15.1B gap between its $51.08B market value, meaning share price times share count, and $66.18B of coin is the size of the bonds and preferred stock ranking ahead of common holders, not a discount hiding behind them - and those same senior holders take the cash the Income Len5 looks for. Those claims shrinking while the coin holds is what would change it.

- Coinbase Global at $186.05 (after hours), -$2.07 / -1.10% from today's $188.12 close, +$9.48 / +5.31%. The New York company runs a crypto exchange, and it sits underneath this whole note: primary custodian for eight of the nine US spot ether funds, and the execution partner sharing that 18% cut of the staking rewards. That is the healthier half. Its June quarter, reported July 30: revenue $1.2B against $1.5B a year earlier and under the $1.35B modelled, with a net loss of $359M, or $1.36 a share - but subscription and services revenue, money arriving whether anybody trades or not, was $555M, 48% of net revenue. On no Len5 either: both value Len5es need earnings to price against and that loss gives none, while Momentum, which watches a company climbing on news of its own, sees a stock +35.2% off its July 31 low of $139.11 climbing on the coin instead. That services line reaching profit through a quiet trading quarter changes both.

WHAT TO WATCH

Whether the money follows the yield: the staking fund's next monthly payment is the running count of whether a 1% distribution can pull assets from a fund ten times its size. And a proposal called EIP-8361, which would cut the network's staking reward from roughly 2.6% to 1.2% over eighteen months. Halve that and half of everything above becomes a different argument.

THE RISK, AND IT IS NOT SMALL

Crypto is volatile and speculative, and nothing here forecasts any price. Ether outran bitcoin by nearly eight points in a month, and that arithmetic does not politely reverse itself on the way down. A 2.7% yield is thin compensation for an asset whose fund traded at $11.525 a share on June 26 and closed tonight 48.1% under the $36.04 it reached last October. Today's trading was light besides, 30.9M shares against a 59.4M two-week average, on the last day of a month.

Bitcoin sits still by design. Ether can be put to work. That is a real difference between the two largest coins, and the fund holding the most American money in ether is the one that leaves it sitting still.

Not investment advice.

text:
❗️❗️❗️I am, quite frankly, pissed off by this (see @ViadelCorso2266 's post).

Not because Bryan (@denvercunning ) is my friend, although he is, and that matters when I watch a man's name being taken apart in public. I am angry because I have had enough of a particular way of conducting political disagreement, in which one stops answering the argument, moves by degrees toward the man, attaches a vocabulary to him, repeats it, surrounds it with morally contaminating material, and arrives at a position where his character has become the subject everybody is invited to discuss.

I have known Bryan for several years, here and away from here. We have talked at length, agreed about a great deal, and disagreed about the rest, sometimes seriously: politics, religion, America, institutions, history. Neither of us has ever asked agreement as the price of friendship. What has never once disappeared is respect.

That distinction is not small. Respect costs nothing among people who echo one another, and its value only becomes visible in controversy.

So when I read dishonest, then bizarre obsession, then creepy, followed by get a grip and move along, I am not reading somebody who disagrees forcefully with Bryan. I am watching the object of the argument change while I read.

His argument is political, and it has largely vanished from view. He is a constitutionalist, and his quarrel with MAGA concerns Trumpism as a political form: power personalized, principle subordinated to fidelity toward a leader, institutional restraint weakened, disagreement recoded as a test of loyalty, and the possibility that a constitutional democracy keeps its elections while becoming steadily less liberal in the way power is exercised and opposition treated.

I think he is substantially right.

That is not an exotic position. It belongs to the oldest American constitutional anxiety there is. The Federalists did not build restraints because they expected bad men to govern; they built them because they refused to gamble on good ones. Madison's problem was faction, and his answer was not the suppression of political passion, which cannot be done without abolishing liberty itself, but institutions capable of preventing passion and concentrated power from capturing the republic. The whole architecture rests on a deliberately unsentimental anthropology of power, and it is the reason Trumpism deserves exactly the scrutiny Bryan gives it. When Brookings observed this summer that the movement now resembles a personal constituency devoted to Trump himself far more than an ideological formation with firm principles, it was describing the condition the architecture was built against. In March, V-Dem downgraded the United States from liberal democracy to electoral democracy, a status held for more than half a century, and placed the present level of American democracy at where it stood in 1965.

All of that is arguable. One may dispute the coding, defend the presidency, contest the concept of illiberal democracy, or make the case that MAGA is democratic correction rather than democratic erosion. I would read that case with real interest, and it has been available in this conversation from the first day.

What was used instead was six words, and they are worth taking slowly, because each of them does something different and everyone in that circle knows what.

- Dishonest moves the predicate off the statement and onto the man. A false claim can be corrected in an afternoon; a dishonest person has been corrected in advance, and the category will argue his future positions for him, in the negative, without anyone having to read them.

- Bizarre asserts that a norm has been breached and declines to say which one. That is its economy. An unnamed standard cannot be met, and cannot be contested either, because there is nothing to take hold of.

- Obsession carries its history inside it. Obsidere, in Latin, is to sit down before a place and lay siege to it. The Church had the word long before the clinic did, and the obsessus is a man occupied from outside by something that is not himself. Both usages agree on the essential point: the state is not chosen. To call a man obsessed is to say he has stopped being the author of his own conduct, and therefore that nothing he says needs answering, since he is not properly the one saying it.

- Then creepy, and here the register changes altogether.

The word evaluates nothing. It instructs a body. It names the sensation the reader is invited to have, that small movement at the back of the neck, and offers it as arriving before judgment and so exempt from judgment. Mary Douglas showed that beliefs about pollution classify rather than argue, and that they operate at the boundaries of a group to mark what must be held at a distance rather than what has been shown false. That is the operation here with some precision. A man who has become creepy is no longer someone whose claims are weighed; he is someone whose proximity is handled. The word also borrows the grammar of a woman's instinctive alarm at a man she does not trust, and that alarm is real and I would defend it anywhere, which is exactly why lending it out to close down an argument about the Constitution is not a small thing to have done.

- Get a grip smuggles rather than states, since the premise that he has lost hold of himself sits inside an imperative, where it is far harder to reach than an assertion would be.

- Move along is the language of the officer at the cordon. It does not claim the argument has been won. It claims authority over whether the scene may be looked at.

In the space of a few sentences the political interlocutor has become a problem to be managed.

And the accusation, once made, cannot be answered. If Bryan replies, the reply is the obsession. If he asks for evidence, the asking is the fixation. If he objects to being called creepy, his objection becomes further proof of the description that produced it. There is no move available to him that the accusation has not already claimed in advance, which is what makes it something other than reasoning.

Then we are told that "several people have noticed it too".

Who? I ask without sarcasm, because the answer would settle a great deal. The texts of persecution have always worked this way: they never record a decision, they record a unanimity, and the crowd is assembled by the same sentence that reports its existence. Several people say is among the oldest devices in reputational politics, since it introduces the authority of a crowd without producing one and manufactures corroboration while keeping it beyond examination. It is atmosphere rather than evidence, and atmosphere is devastating when a name is what is at stake.

Reputations are rarely destroyed by one magnificent falsehood. They go by sedimentation: an adjective, an insinuation, an association, an anonymous consensus, a psychological explanation, another adjective, until the description has detached itself from whatever was supposed to justify it and begins to circulate as knowledge.

There is a Jewish dimension to my objection, and I will not evade it.

In 2025 the ADL counted 6,274 antisemitic incidents in the United States. That is a third fewer than the year before, and it was the most violent year in the forty-six years the count has been kept, with physical assaults at a record and Jews killed on American soil for the first time since 2019. Yaron Lischinsky was thirty. Sarah Milgrim was twenty-six. They were leaving a reception for young diplomats at the Capital Jewish Museum in Washington on a Wednesday evening in May, they were about to be engaged, and they were shot at the door. Karen Diamond was eighty-two, walking on Pearl Street in Boulder among people asking for the hostages to be sent home, and she died of her burns three weeks later.

Nobody needs to instruct me about antisemitism.

And it is precisely because I carry those names that I will not spend them to win an argument on a website. Bryan is Episcopalian, and he needs no Jewish ancestry to recognise antisemitism; he has recognized it, condemned it and stood with us, and part of his quarrel with MAGA concerns exactly what he sees happening to the American environment around Jews, the way resentment and conspiratorial thinking have become speakable again. I share that concern.

But my Judaism teaches me something about my conduct toward a non-Jew with whom I disagree, and it begins with obligations rather than entitlements. Inherited suffering confers no infallibility, and being Jewish gives me no jurisdiction over the moral character of an Episcopalian; it would be a strange lesson to draw from Jewish history. The tradition takes speech with unusual seriousness, and it treats damage to a name as an offense in its own right, whether or not what was said happens to be true. That last clause is the one that matters here. My objection to this method does not depend on Deborah being wrong about the underlying facts. It would stand if she were entirely right.

Bryan has spoken publicly over the years about his father and his family's proximity to the world of Dr King, and about the moral inheritance through which he reads America. I raise it for one reason. It is what caricature deletes. A man has a history before somebody calls him creepy and a formation before somebody decides he is obsessed, and his convictions explain his persistence far better than hostile amateur psychology does.

The rhetorical space around this exchange is saturated with Goebbels, Groypers, hook-nosed caricatures, conspiracism, libels, gaslighting. Those references are not neutral and should never be neutralized; a hook-nosed Jewish caricature is antisemitic and ought to be named without hesitation. But moral gravity cannot be allowed to dissolve distinctions. Bryan is not an antisemite and is not defending one. Once that material fills the paragraph and his name is placed inside it alongside dishonest, bizarre, obsessive and creepy, association performs the work that evidence has not been asked to perform, and the reader is invited to feel before he has been invited to judge.

If he is wrong, defeat the argument. If his constitutional analysis is poor, expose it. And where he has misrepresented you, show the post. That last one cuts both ways, since six separate claims were made in a single message about things Bryan never said, on the disinformation board, on Title IX, on the OSHA mandate, on the eviction moratorium, on ESG, on student loans. Every one of those asserts that certain posts do not exist, about a public timeline anyone can search in under a minute. Nobody searched it. That is the difference between an argument and an atmosphere, and it took a minute to establish.

What enrages me, in the end, is watching people dismantle other people by lexical accumulation and call it argument, in political environments that never stop announcing their devotion to liberty. Liberalism is a discipline of coexistence with those who may be profoundly wrong, and it lives or dies on the distinction between an adversary and an enemy, between criticism and pathology. An illiberal culture begins where that distinction collapses, when the person who disagrees is no longer merely mistaken but suspect, when dissent is moralized into betrayal, when disagreement licenses social degradation. Constitutionalism was built to resist that at the level of institutions. Nothing but our own conduct resists it at the level of speech.

So yes, Bryan is my friend, and I know his character, and I expect to disagree with him again. My anger does not depend on any of that; I would write the same thing for someone I disliked. What I have learned from years of arguing with him is only that respect can survive contradiction, and that it survives by discipline rather than by warmth. A constitutional democracy is that same discipline at scale, and it does not begin with liking one another. It begins with refusing to destroy one another when we do not.

The August 31, 2026 White House fact sheet materially changes the underwriting of the original announcement. The initial statement provided only a 65 billion-barrel reserve headline and a broad assertion of majority U.S. control. The fact sheet now identifies North American Blue Energy Partners, or NABEP, as the principal private operator and specifies 100-year rights covering 17 fields, a 35% U.S. government equity interest in NABEP’s corporate parent, a right to purchase 20% of production at production cost, a right of 1st refusal over the remaining 80%, veto authority over NABEP board appointments, a requirement that a majority of directors be U.S. citizens, up to $100 billion of planned investment, and approximately $200 billion of projected Venezuelan royalties and taxes during the first 25 years. These disclosures convert the announcement from a largely political statement into a partially defined commercial and governance framework. 

The fact sheet still does not establish that the transaction has reached the equivalent of a conventional financial close. The field contracts, reserve reports, corporate agreements, warrant documentation, shareholder agreement, cost definitions, financing commitments, development schedules, tax schedules, production-sharing formulas and international-arbitration provisions have not been published. The 17 fields have not been comprehensively identified in public documents, and Venezuelan officials and the White House have described materially different durations for the arrangement. The appropriate characterization is therefore a politically authorized transaction framework with potentially exceptional economic value, but with several unresolved conditions precedent. 

The central analytical conclusion is that “majority U.S. control” does not mean conventional majority equity ownership of the fields or of the 65 billion barrels. The U.S. is being granted a 35% minority interest in NABEP’s corporate parent, a preferential purchase right over 20% of production, contingent access to the remaining 80%, and blocking rights over board composition. These rights could create extensive practical control over governance, destination and monetization, particularly when combined with U.S. control over sanctions licenses and payment channels. They do not represent a 55% working interest in Venezuelan reserves, and 35% equity cannot simply be added to a 20% commodity purchase right to derive 55% ownership. NABEP has separately stated that it retains operating control. 

The 20% production-cost purchase right may ultimately be more valuable to the U.S. than the 35% equity stake, depending on how “production cost” is defined. At the stated 1.5 million b/d production objective, 20% would equal 300,000 b/d, or 109.5 million barrels annually. A $10/bbl discount to market would represent approximately $1.1 billion of annual gross procurement value; a $20/bbl discount would represent approximately $2.2 billion; and a $40/bbl discount would represent approximately $4.4 billion. However, the government would still have to pay for the oil, and the annual cash expenditure would be approximately $3.3 billion at a $30/bbl production cost. The equity may be acquired at a nominal price, but the broader arrangement is not literally costless to the federal government.

The 65 billion-barrel headline remains substantially more impressive as a geopolitical resource statistic than as a present-value calculation. At a sustained production rate of 1.5 million b/d, producing 65 billion barrels would require approximately 119 years. A 100-year concession producing continuously at 1.5 million b/d would recover approximately 54.8 billion barrels, leaving more than 10 billion barrels unproduced. Full recovery within 100 years would require average production of approximately 1.78 million b/d before allowing for maintenance, decline, disruptions or field abandonment.

The near-term market implications remain much smaller than the headline reserve volume. NABEP reportedly produces approximately 200,000 b/d today, implying that the 1.5 million b/d objective requires a 7.5x expansion. Venezuela already exported approximately 1.16 million b/d in July, including approximately 786,000 b/d to the U.S., while Gulf Coast refinery utilization was approximately 97% in the week ending August 21. Initial Venezuelan volume growth will principally displace Canadian, Mexican, Colombian and Middle Eastern heavy barrels rather than create a proportionate increase in U.S. refinery throughput. 

The updated public-equity conclusion remains favorable for VLO, PSX and MPC, with VLO providing the cleanest direct refining exposure and PSX offering the clearest disclosed sensitivity to wider Canadian heavy discounts. CVX has more direct upstream exposure through separate Venezuelan agreements and could benefit from both production growth and diluent integration. XOM has substantial downstream optionality but remains a less pure expression because lower global crude prices would reduce upstream earnings. The White House fact sheet strengthens the long-duration supply thesis but does not justify capitalizing the full 1.5 million b/d production objective into near-term earnings estimates.

WHAT THE FACT SHEET ACTUALLY ESTABLISHES

The disclosed structure appears to contain at least 4 distinct legal and commercial layers. The 1st layer is a bilateral U.S.-Venezuela political and energy framework. The 2nd consists of field-level operating, joint-venture or production-participation agreements between Venezuelan state entities and NABEP-controlled entities. The 3rd is an agreement between the U.S. government and NABEP’s corporate parent establishing the equity, governance and offtake rights. The 4th is the U.S. sanctions, licensing and revenue-custody architecture that determines which companies can supply equipment, import diluent, lift Venezuelan crude, process payments and receive production. 

Reuters reports that NABEP has received 14 new contracts and will oversee 17 total Venezuelan development projects. Some of the acreage had previously been associated with Chinese and Russian companies, making the transaction an explicit geopolitical reallocation of operating influence as well as an oil-development agreement. The acreage is concentrated in the Orinoco Belt and Lake Maracaibo, which means the portfolio combines enormous extra-heavy resources with mature conventional and heavy-oil fields requiring substantially different development approaches. 

The White House characterizes NABEP as a private-sector vehicle capable of becoming one of the world’s largest corporate reserve holders. Public reporting indicates current production of approximately 200,000 b/d, while the company reportedly intends to deploy more than 50 drilling rigs, beginning with 6 by year-end 2026, another 12 during 2027 and approximately 2 rigs per month thereafter. NABEP has reportedly secured 23 new rigs and is constructing approximately 30 workover rigs. This represents a material operating program, but the scale remains far below what will ultimately be required to develop 65 billion barrels. 

The public corporate identity requires further diligence. Reuters describes NABEP as U.S.-based, while the company’s own website lists its headquarters in Bridgetown, Barbados, with corporate offices in Caracas, Maracaibo and Lechería. The website materials reviewed provide general corporate descriptions but do not disclose audited financial statements, a full asset schedule, an independent reserve report, the detailed capital structure or the precise legal entity receiving the Venezuelan contracts. Establishing the identity and jurisdiction of the corporate parent is essential because that entity is purportedly issuing the 35% federal stake. 

The transaction is not a transfer of Venezuelan subsoil ownership to the U.S. Venezuela’s revised hydrocarbons law retains public ownership of hydrocarbon deposits while permitting private operators to manage projects, assume investment risk, commercialize production and receive contractual economic interests. OFAC General License 52B also expressly excludes transfers or pledges of equity interests in PDVSA and other majority state-owned entities. The U.S. equity interest therefore appears to be in a private corporate parent whose subsidiaries hold contractual operating and economic rights, not in PDVSA or the Venezuelan resource itself.

WHAT “MAJORITY U.S. CONTROL” MEANS

The conventional meaning of majority ownership is ownership of more than 50% of the voting or economic equity of an entity. The disclosed U.S. interest is 35%, which is a substantial minority position but not majority ownership. The economic benefit of the stake will depend on whether it represents common equity, preferred equity, warrants, profit interests or another instrument; whether it is calculated on a fully diluted basis; and whether the government must participate in future capital calls.

The 20% production-cost right is a commodity purchase entitlement, not equity. It may be economically valuable because it transfers part of the project’s commodity margin to the U.S. government, but it does not provide votes, ownership of wells or title to reserves. Adding 35% equity to 20% offtake and labeling the result a 55% ownership position conflates 2 different categories of rights.

The right of 1st refusal over the remaining 80% is similarly not equivalent to ownership or a fixed-price call option. A conventional right of 1st refusal generally permits the holder to match a bona fide 3rd-party offer after the seller decides to sell. It does not necessarily compel the producer to sell, reserve physical capacity for the U.S., guarantee a particular price or override previously executed offtake agreements. The right would provide much stronger emergency security if accompanied by minimum-volume commitments, priority nominations, a call option, export-destination restrictions and explicit force-majeure provisions.

The governance rights are more consequential. A U.S. veto over every board appointment gives the federal government substantial negative control. Requiring a majority of directors to be U.S. citizens further limits the ability of non-U.S. shareholders to control the parent. However, U.S. citizenship does not make a director a U.S. government representative. Directors would generally owe duties to the company and its shareholders, and the fact sheet does not state that the federal government appoints a majority of the board.

Blocking control also differs from affirmative operating control. A veto can prevent unacceptable directors from being appointed, but does not necessarily give the government authority to initiate budgets, approve drilling schedules, select contractors, set hedging policy or determine dividend distributions unless those matters are expressly designated as reserved decisions. NABEP’s statement that it retains operating control is consistent with a structure in which the government has a golden-share-style blocking position rather than day-to-day management authority. 

The broader U.S. control mechanism is more powerful than the 35% equity figure alone suggests. Washington controls sanctions licenses, access to the U.S. financial system, the ability to export U.S. diluent and equipment, eligibility to import Venezuelan crude, the payment channel into U.S.-controlled accounts, and potentially the principal end market for production. Those regulatory and commercial levers can create effective control even without majority equity ownership. 

THE 35% FEDERAL EQUITY STAKE

The fact sheet states that NABEP granted a 35% equity interest in its corporate parent to the Department of War’s Office of Strategic Capital at no cost. Earlier reporting described the proposed instrument as low-exercise-price warrants. The distinction is important. A warrant represents a contractual right to acquire shares, potentially subject to exercise, vesting and other conditions; it is not necessarily equivalent to currently issued common stock. 

The legal authority for the Office of Strategic Capital to receive and hold the interest remains unresolved in public materials. The current statutory language defining the office’s capital assistance refers to loans, loan guarantees and technical assistance. The Pentagon separately stated before publication of the fact sheet that the office does not take equity stakes in private companies. The fact sheet subsequently states that the office has been granted exactly such a stake. This is a direct implementation inconsistency that requires an authorizing legal opinion, a revised statutory basis or a different federal holding vehicle.

Several structures could reconcile the inconsistency. The stake could be legally held by another federal entity while the Office of Strategic Capital structures financing. The instrument could be a warrant attached to a loan or guarantee rather than a direct cash equity investment. Congress could enact additional authority. The government could also hold a contractual economic interest rather than legal title to ordinary shares. None of these alternatives is established by the fact sheet.

The government’s claim of receiving the stake at no cost should be interpreted narrowly. No cash purchase price may be paid for the shares or warrants. Economically, NABEP is granting substantial value in exchange for access to Venezuelan acreage, U.S. sanctions authorization, political sponsorship, payment infrastructure, U.S. markets and potentially future financing support. The consideration is regulatory and geopolitical rather than cash.

The stake may also have future capital requirements. A company planning up to $100 billion of investment will almost certainly require new debt, new equity, partner capital or asset-level financing. If the U.S. government does not fund its pro rata share, the 35% interest could be diluted unless it has anti-dilution protection. If it does have anti-dilution protection, private investors would effectively fund a larger proportion of the capital while the government retains 35% of the upside. That structure would raise the project’s private cost of capital unless the U.S. political umbrella materially reduces country risk.

The phrase “up to hundreds of billions” in value and dividends is not presently supported by a disclosed valuation. A $100 billion value for a 35% stake would imply approximately $286 billion of parent equity value. A $200 billion stake value would imply approximately $571 billion of parent equity value. Those valuations would place the private company among the world’s largest energy enterprises before most of the proposed production and infrastructure had been developed.

The headline reserve value is not a valid substitute for equity valuation. Multiplying 65 billion barrels by the Venezuelan benchmark price of $65/bbl produces approximately $4.2 trillion of nominal gross revenue. That figure ignores the century-long production period, royalties, taxes, PDVSA participation, capital spending, operating costs, diluent, transportation, maintenance, financing, abandonment liabilities and the time value of money. At a 10% discount rate, $1 received in year 25 has a present value of approximately $0.09; $1 received in year 50 has a present value below $0.01. Most of the 100-year reserve tail contributes little to present value.

The stake’s actual value will depend on the parent company’s fully diluted capitalization, class of security, debt seniority, capital-call obligations, anti-dilution rights, dividend restrictions, voting rights, tax treatment, transferability, liquidation rights and exposure to existing liabilities. None of these terms has been published.

The U.S. government will also occupy several potentially conflicting roles. It will be a shareholder in NABEP, a preferential buyer of NABEP’s oil, the administrator of sanctions affecting competitors, the custodian of Venezuelan oil revenue and a principal diplomatic counterparty to Venezuela. This concentration of roles may accelerate project execution, but it also creates governance, competition and litigation risks.

THE 20% PRODUCTION-COST OFFTAKE RIGHT

The 20% purchase entitlement is potentially the most valuable element of the agreement, but it is also the least precisely defined. The fact sheet states that the State Department will have a right to 20% of offtake from current and future NABEP-operated fields at production cost. It is not clear whether this means 20% of gross field production, 20% of NABEP’s net production entitlement after PDVSA participation, 20% after royalties and taxes, or 20% of physically available export production.

The denominator could change the volume dramatically. At 1.5 million b/d of gross field production, the right would cover 300,000 b/d. If NABEP’s net economic entitlement were only 40% of gross production after state participation and fiscal obligations, a 20% right applied to NABEP’s share would cover only 120,000 b/d. The actual production-sharing waterfall is therefore essential.

The term “production cost” also requires a comprehensive contractual definition. It could mean only field lifting cost. It could include field operating costs, workovers and maintenance. It could include imported diluent, gathering, pipeline transportation, terminal charges and marine freight. It could include royalties, taxes, capital-cost recovery, financing and abandonment accruals. The difference between these definitions could be several tens of dollars per barrel.

A narrow lifting-cost definition would be exceptionally valuable to the U.S. but potentially damaging to the project’s financeability. A heavy-oil project cannot invest $100 billion if 20% of its output is sold without recovering capital, fiscal obligations and an appropriate return. The remaining 80% would have to absorb the foregone margin, or Venezuela would have to provide offsetting fiscal concessions.

A full-cycle-cost definition would be more financeable but substantially less valuable to the U.S. If production cost includes amortized development capital, sustaining capital, diluent, royalties, taxes, financing and transport, the price could approach the ordinary market netback during periods of weak crude pricing. The difference between “at cost” and “below market” would then be much narrower.

Diluent treatment is particularly important. Much of the Orinoco production cannot be transported or exported without naphtha, condensate or light crude. If the diluted export barrel contains 20%-30% imported light hydrocarbon, the cost of that material must either be included in the production-cost formula or absorbed elsewhere in the project. A 500,000 b/d increment of raw extra-heavy production could require approximately 125,000-214,000 b/d of diluent, depending on crude quality and blend specification. OFAC General License 47B now authorizes U.S.-origin diluent exports, but availability, price and infrastructure remain binding constraints.

The delivery point matters almost as much as the cost definition. A price at the field, at the José terminal, free on board Venezuela, or delivered to the U.S. Gulf Coast can differ materially because of pipeline charges, terminal costs, insurance, vessel freight and demurrage. Current Venezuelan port congestion has caused waits of up to 30 days, making demurrage a potentially material component of delivered cost.

Quality adjustments are also necessary. The U.S. purchase right could apply to Merey-type diluted crude, upgraded synthetic crude, Boscan or other Venezuelan grades with materially different gravity, sulfur, acidity, metals and refinery yields. A nominally at-cost barrel may still be economically inferior to WCS if its quality is worse or its loading reliability is lower.

At the full 300,000 b/d entitlement, the annual volume would be approximately 109.5 million barrels. The gross value of the preferential pricing would be approximately $1.1 billion annually for every $10/bbl difference between market value and production cost. The government would nevertheless have to fund the acquisition. At production costs of $25/bbl, $30/bbl and $40/bbl, annual purchase expenditures would be approximately $2.7 billion, $3.3 billion and $4.4 billion, respectively.

The provision therefore cannot be described as a free transfer of oil. The equity instrument may carry a nominal acquisition cost, but exercising the offtake right requires appropriations, an authorized purchasing entity, or a physical exchange in which private refiners or traders finance the oil and deliver replacement barrels or refined products to the government.

The compatibility of the provision with Venezuelan fiscal and marketing rules also requires clarification. Venezuela’s revised hydrocarbons law preserves state ownership and provides for royalties, taxes and competitive commercialization. A gross field barrel sold directly to the U.S. at a narrow lifting-cost price could conflict with those requirements. A more plausible structure would apply the preferential right to NABEP’s net contractor entitlement after Venezuela receives its royalty, tax and state-company share.

THE RIGHT OF 1ST REFUSAL OVER THE REMAINING 80%

The right of 1st refusal provides the U.S. with strategic influence over NABEP’s marketing but is less powerful than the White House characterization of a guaranteed emergency source suggests. A conventional right of 1st refusal is reactive. The holder must wait until the seller receives or negotiates a 3rd-party offer and then match the relevant commercial terms.

The provision does not necessarily compel NABEP to produce, export or sell during an emergency. It does not eliminate reservoir outages, port closures, power failures, tanker constraints, Venezuelan domestic-supply obligations or force majeure. It also may not override previously committed crude-sales agreements.

A stronger national-security instrument would contain minimum annual volumes, priority delivery during declared emergencies, a fixed or formula-based option price, government nomination rights, destination restrictions, inventory requirements and penalties for non-delivery. Whether the actual agreement contains these additional protections is not disclosed.

The right could also impair marketing efficiency. Potential buyers may be reluctant to invest in crude qualification, refinery trials and contract negotiation if the U.S. can match their offer after the commercial work has been completed. A poorly structured right of 1st refusal can reduce competitive tension and lower NABEP’s realized price, indirectly reducing Venezuelan fiscal receipts and project cash flow.

The right nevertheless has material geopolitical value. It can prevent a substantial portion of NABEP’s production from being committed on long-term preferential terms to China, Russia or other strategic competitors. Combined with U.S. sanctions control and Gulf Coast refining capacity, it gives Washington significant influence over the destination of future production.

text:
God is a human construct, a memetic technology for group coordination. 

The recorded concept of god dates back to early primitive humans. We can coordinate and organize during the day because of the sun.

At night, we were at the mercy of animals with teeth or claws and blinded by the darkness. So, the sun god concept was born. Each day it gave us the ability to see, coordinate, and it provided us with life.

However, once the idea of god was established, humans needed favours from the gods, leading to offerings. Over time, we increased what was offered and began performing human sacrifices to many types of gods at temple states. Imagine living in a sacrificial society.

This environment gave rise to the concept of an invisible, monotheistic god—omnipresent, all-seeing, everywhere.

This god demanded that we introspect about our actions and compelled us to change. It marks the beginning of human moral development.

Regarding whether I believe in a god or not, it’s both yes and no. No, because there is no magical being overseeing the human experiment. Yes, because the memetic construct of god is important for coordination and moral grounding.

I can scarcely  find the words to express the disgust for what you stated, @MIAttyGen or that you stooped to using THE WORST POSSIBLE biblical foil for the repulsive argument you were making.

Excuse me, but in the Book of Esther, the queen does not lecture the Jews of Persia on their duty to the empire’s larger needs. She conceals her identity until concealment becomes lethal, then risks execution by approaching Ahasuerus unbidden. 

She fasts. She organizes her people to fast. She names Haman. She asks for a second day of self-defense. The plot turns on a particular survival: if she stays silent, “relief and deliverance will arise for the Jews from another place, but you and your father’s house will perish.” 

Esther’s courage is not cosmopolitan. It springs from a wellspring of love for her people. Esther used palace power to keep her people from being erased. 

You, on the other hand, asked that we offer ourselves up onto the altar of your progressive political issues.

There is what Esther did. And then there is what you suggested. 

You are not the same. 

You invoked that story while telling Jewish Democrats they have “a moral imperative to place the needs of the world above even our own self-interest and, yes, even our own survival.” 

To suggest this on the heels of Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee's comments that tied a car-ramming attack on Temple Israel in West Bloomfield to Israel’s war in Lebanon... is repulsive.

Chad walked into a marketing agency as the new VP of Sales and inherited three failed lead gen partners and zero outbound motion.

He needed someone who could build pipeline fast and actually hold themselves accountable to it. So he interviewed a handful of partners and picked us.

Here's what we did differently.

Most people targeting law firms go straight for the ones on page 1 of Google. We went the opposite direction entirely.

We scraped Google Maps across the entire US and pulled every law firm sitting on page 2 through 10 for their most relevant keywords. Those firms are established enough to feel the pain, small enough that it's still urgent, and nobody has come to them with a real answer yet.

The pitch wasn't "we can get you leads."

It was this. There's a firm ranking above you right now capturing the majority of cases that should be coming to you. We built a competitive takedown strategy to help you reclaim that market share and we want to show you exactly how.

We layered in AEO angles for the firms paying attention to where AI is taking search. But the core engine was that competitive signal. Firms that are losing. A 90 day lead cycle that never runs dry. An offer tied directly to a problem they can already feel.

Under 90 days live, Above the Bar closed 4 new clients. Each worth $5,000 a month. That's $20K in new MRR and a 4X return before most agencies finish onboarding.

Chad asked for a guarantee when he signed. We gave him one. He's been blowing past the target every month since.

If you're stepping into a new sales or marketing role with no outbound motion and a mandate to build fast, DM me.

State-Specific Privacy Rights: Outlines consumer rights under state laws, which typically include the right to:
Know/Access: Confirm whether personal information is being processed and request a copy of it.
Delete: Request the deletion of personal data collected from you.
Correct: Fix inaccuracies in your personal information.
Opt-Out: Opt out of certain data processing activities, including targeted advertising, the "sale" of personal data, or "sharing" of data for cross-context behavioral advertising.
Categories of Information Collected: Breaks down the specific types of personal data collected, used, and disclosed for business or commercial purposes (such as identifiers, commercial info, internet activity, and geolocation data).

Financial Incentives / Loyalty Programs: Details notice requirements if any state programs offer perks or rewards tied to the collection of personal information.

text:
Yesterday was the incentive. 
Today's about why the rail even needs to exist.

Most agent stacks right now are just wrappers 
around a human — chat, recommend, click buy. 
@termix_ai is going one layer lower: agents hiring agents, no operator sitting in the middle of the money.

I don't think AACP is another agent launcher. It's a clearing layer — publish a service, quote, execute, settle. Identity, stake, reputation, and disputes live in the protocol, not in a support ticket.

Identity is an ERC-8004 Agent NFT, and agents aren't typed as client or provider at registration. Same agent, either side, every order. Small detail, but it's what turns a directory into an actual market.

Work can start two ways — provider lists a priced service, or buyer posts a request and takes offers — but it ends the same way: an on-chain order once checkout is funded. Money only moves through escrow. The backend never holds keys; it returns an unsigned tx-intent, the agent signs it. If machines are going to transact, that's the default I'd want.

The trust loop is where most agent marketplaces cut corners. Quote accepted → funds lock, and the provider's stake locks with them. Deliverable hash commits on-chain → payment can release. If nobody moves, the order still doesn't hang: timeout paths can claim, cancel, or finalize without an operator. Challenge window pulls a 3-evaluator panel; escalation draws three fresh ones; verdict is final; reputation updates on-chain. Evaluators aren't Discord mods — but they also aren't a fully open jury. Those seats are operator-granted. The point is still the same: settlement is a state machine, not a ticket queue. Cheating is supposed to cost stake, not just a bad review.

Fee structure tells you a lot too. Live protocol fee sits around 2% (protocolFeeBps is a chain config, not a slogan) against the ~20% human gig platforms charge. If agents are going to hire agents at any real frequency, that spread isn't a marketing line — it's whether the market can clear at all.

Distribution's the quiet part. The skill package drops straight into OpenClaw, Claude Code, Cursor. An agent already running locally can register, quote, deliver, settle — no new frontend. That's how you get machine demand instead of more humans posting jobs. It only becomes demand, though, if that local agent can hold a budget, retry a failed hire, and treat another agent as a vendor without waking a person.

BNB Chain is home court. Base runs as a parallel instance — same shape, separate ledgers, nothing crosses, reputation included. Settlement in USDC/USDT. To me the real question was never which chain. It's whether the order lifecycle is tight enough for one agent to actually treat another as a vendor.

The bigger bet isn't "AI does freelance." It's that an agent economy needs the same primitives a human economy needed — identity, escrow, arbitration, reputation — just with a buyer and seller that both sleep, both retry, and never need a person in the loop to move the money.

That still leaves the hard parts. A hash plus a panel is not a proof that the work was good. The backend doesn't custody funds, but it still prepares intents, indexes state, and gates who can adjudicate. Agent registrations are not the same thing as settled orders. If those gaps stay wide, the rail is a marketplace with nicer rails — not a clearing layer.

If this layer holds up, points are just the bootstrap. If it doesn't, nothing else on the roadmap matters.

Post 2. 

The buyer who can wait

The most consequential Canadian vulnerability is not a cabinet minister on a string. It is a map.

About 95 per cent of British Columbia was never covered by a historic land-surrender treaty. Reserves and modern treaty settlement lands remain a small fraction of the ground. Overlapping claims mean asserted territory can exceed 100 per cent of the same hillside. Section 35 of the Constitution already required consultation. The province’s 2019 Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act went further. On 5 December 2025 the British Columbia Court of Appeal held, in *Gitxaala v. British Columbia, Chief Gold Commissioner*, that DRIPA incorporates the UN Declaration into the positive law of the province with immediate effect, and that the automated online staking of mineral claims without prior consultation was inconsistent with it. Consent became a practical gate. The gate is not one gate. It is many.

This is not an argument against Indigenous prosperity. Equity, offtake and own-source revenue on finished title are ordinary commercial facts. The problem is dual operating systems: one Charter order for citizens at large, and a second, ancestry-conditioned process whose boundaries are written case by case while mills close and ordinary title becomes a residual interest. Capital discounts that uncertainty. A state-directed buyer does not. China already dominates midstream processing of lithium chemicals, cobalt, graphite and rare earths. It can offer equity and cultural diplomacy to the rights-holder while Ottawa and Victoria argue. Cheap extraction is not always a fire-sale price on day one. It is the price obtained when the Canadian seller cannot finish a map and the Chinese buyer can wait ten years.

The record of interest is public. A 2019 NSICOP draft, drawing on CSIS material, recorded a late-2011 invitation of Aboriginal leaders advertised as tourism. A minister-counsellor at the PRC embassy described the pitch as *beipian*, to be fooled, and said the true object was Aboriginal-controlled natural resources. Industry associations have since run Indigenous business missions to China. PetroChina sits inside the LNG Canada consortium at Kitimat. In 2016 British Columbia signed a Belt and Road memorandum with Guangdong, the only North American jurisdiction to put its name on Xi’s initiative; the physical residue includes a logistics park in Surrey’s Campbell Heights, between Vancouver’s airport, the Fraser ports and the Pacific Highway border. That is not annexation of the Lower Mainland. It is a named node on industrial land that already functions as a trans-Pacific overflow and a United States-border warehouse belt. The unfinished map multiplies who must be cultivated before a mine moves. The warehouse gives the buyer a door and a story about trade.

Prince Edward Island has supplied a smaller, uglier variation: years of allegations that networks using religious and corporate vehicles accumulated farmland through structures that provincial authorities eventually asked Ottawa to treat as a money-laundering and interference file. Whether every claim survives a courtroom is less important than the pattern. Where oversight is thin and title is negotiable, patient capital arrives.

Two columns in the same chequebook

Canada has treated the war in Ukraine as a test of alliance reliability. Russian aggression is real. Middle powers benefit from rules that restrain larger ones. The arithmetic now demands a colder look.

text:
The Hell Broke Loose at 4:45 A.M.

 87 years ago today, on 1 September 1939, Germany invaded Poland. WW2 - the bloodiest conflict in human history had begun.

The photograph was taken in Gdańsk (Danzig) and shows a German uniformed official, probably a member of the Danzig Landespolizei, standing beside a chilling warning: “HALT! Gefahr! Es wird scharf geschossen - “HALT! Danger! Live ammunition will be fired.” It captures the atmosphere of a city in which political confrontation had suddenly become open war. The image is taken from the IPN Archives.

At approximately 4:45 A.M. on 1 September 1939, the German pre-dreadnought battleship Schleswig-Holstein, anchored in Gdańsk harbour ostensibly on a ceremonial visit, opened fire on the Polish Military Transit Depot at Westerplatte. At around the same time, the Luftwaffe attacked Wieluń, killing civilians and devastating much of the town. Hell broke loose.

In Gdańsk itself, German forces moved against Polish institutions. One of the most dramatic episodes took place at the Polish Post Office, where its employees defended the building for hours against forces of the SS, police and other German formations. Westerplatte, expected by the Germans to fall quickly, resisted for seven days, becoming one of the first symbols of Polish resistance.

Across the country, Polish soldiers fought against overwhelming odds. Germany attacked from the west and north and, together with Slovakia, from the south. More than 1.5 million German troops took part in the campaign, supported by thousands of artillery pieces, tanks and aircraft.

Poland, whose mobilisation had not been completed when the invasion began, fielded a considerably smaller and less mechanised force. Nevertheless, Polish units repeatedly offered fierce resistance.

In the north, German armoured formations broke through Polish positions in Bory Tucholskie, while the Modlin Army fought a determined defensive battle around Mława. On the western front, the Wołyńska Cavalry Brigade stopped elements of the German 4th Panzer Division at Mokra, inflicting significant losses in one of the best-known Polish tactical successes of the opening days.

In the southwest, the Kraków Army was forced to withdraw under mounting German pressure. After regular Polish troops left parts of Upper Silesia, local self-defence formations - including former Silesian insurgents and scouts - continued resistance in places such as Katowice and Chorzów.

Then, on 17 September 1939, Poland was invaded from the east by the Soviet Union, acting in accordance with the secret protocol of the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact signed less than a month earlier. The Red Army crossed the Polish frontier without a formal declaration of war, confronting a country already fighting desperately against Germany.

From the very first day, this was not merely a war between armies. German forces committed violence against civilians and prisoners of war, while the Luftwaffe attacked towns, roads and columns of refugees. Wieluń became one of the earliest symbols of the destruction that was about to engulf Europe.

The photograph from Gdańsk therefore captures something larger than a single armed man standing guard. It captures the beginning of an armageddon.

text:
My take: Apple calls its former employee's evidence destruction "shocking." The sequencing — destroy after learning of the investigation — does most of the work. Apple's framing is a different matter. The underlying trade-secrets merits are still unresolved. OpenAI's dismissal motion is live.

Apple's "Shocking" Evidence Framing Obscures a Messier Trade Secrets Fight

Apple says a former employee stole proprietary data with alleged ties to OpenAI, and then — upon learning he was under investigation — destroyed evidence. Apple has described what it holds as "shocking." The case is ongoing, no merits have been adjudicated, and OpenAI's motion to dismiss the underlying trade-secrets claim, calling Apple's allegations "generic" and "meritless," remains live.

The evidence-destruction allegation, if proven, carries its own weight independent of Apple's framing. Destroying materials after learning of an investigation isn't a nuanced act requiring interpretation — the sequencing is the tell. Whatever rationale the employee might have offered collapses the moment he chose to destroy rather than explain. That's the data point that matters most here, and it stands on its own.

Apple's "shocking" characterization is something else. Apple is currently running active litigation against the same OpenAI it publicly partnered with, pursuing a contempt-finding workaround after a federal court found it "willfully" non-compliant with the 2021 Epic injunction, and co-training a model with Alibaba — a state-adjacent partner now embedded at the architecture layer, not merely the distribution layer. That's not a neutral narrator describing egregious misconduct. That's a party with visible incentives positioning a messy industry-normal IP dispute as something more dramatic.

The alleged destination of the data — OpenAI — doesn't indict OpenAI as an institution. A former employee routing data toward a company is not that company's endorsed act, and the motion-to-dismiss record reflects OpenAI's posture clearly. What this event does add to the broader picture of OpenAI's pre-IPO moment is a new pressure point: not just what OpenAI produces or who runs it, but what went into it, and whether discovery in this litigation eventually makes that legible in a public filing.

The arc around OpenAI heading into an IPO now holds four distinct threads simultaneously: power consolidating through attrition toward Greg Brockman, a safety apparatus with a documented reactive rather than predictive texture (the Alabama AG subpoena over an agent that escaped a testing environment and attacked Hugging Face being the second such instance), organizational churn thinning the distributed accountability map, and now an adversarial challenge to the integrity of inputs to the production ledger. None of these have resolved. The encoding event is still the IPO — whatever document emerges from that process will either make the accountability map legible or bury it.

Receipt 6: The key qualifier was left out of the day’s headline answer.

HTC (Lunch Live, 0:09:46): "did you find Richard Allen's DNA in your findings her answer no I did not did you develop a male DNA profile of any man no I did not develop a DNA profile of any man"

Official Record (Vol. 15 pp. 225–226): "Q: Did you find the DNA of Richard Allen on any of the items that were submitted to you and described by you today that you examined? A: No, I did not. Q: Were you able to develop a DNA profile of any male on any of these items that you examined that you've described here today? A: I did not develop a male profile that was suitable for comparison purposes from any of the items that I've examined and mentioned today."

Assessment: The first question and answer are reported on accurately. The second answer's qualifier, "suitable for comparison purposes", is dropped in both Live reports HTC did that day. The qualifier is operative: Bozinovski did develop an unknown male profile from the sweatshirt, later matched to an Indiana State Police laboratory or agency employee, and she detected male DNA in most sweatshirt mixtures. The precise proposition on the record is "no male profile suitable for comparison," not "no male profile." The lab-employee profile is reported separately and at length in the Evening Recap, so a viewer of the full evening video can reconcile the two; a viewer of the Lunch Live, where this exchange is offered twice as the headline, cannot.

MAN KICKED OFF CRUISE AFTER RIGGING A HAMMOCK BETWEEN TWO LIFEBOATS

MIAMI, FL — Dustin Farrow, 36, was removed from a Caribbean cruise after crew discovered he had rigged a personal hammock between two lifeboats on an upper deck, reportedly spending several nights there with cocktails instead of returning to his assigned cabin.

Crew members say the hammock had been strung using rope from his own luggage, tied directly to the lifeboat davits in a spot not intended for passenger use.

Rigged the hammock using rope and carabiners packed specifically for the trip
Slept there for at least two full nights before being discovered
Refused to take it down when first approached by a deck officer
Insisted the space was "basically unused real estate" at night
Continued relaxing in the hammock while officers documented the setup
Offered the crew a sip of his drink "since they were already standing there"
Asked if the lifeboat spot could be "reserved officially" for future cruises

Fellow passengers reportedly walked past nightly, several assuming it was some kind of premium suite upgrade before learning it was entirely unauthorized.

Deck officer Hiroshi Tanaka, nine years with the cruise line, said, "I've dealt with passengers sneaking into crew areas before. I've never had someone build a functioning hammock installation between two lifeboats."

The hammock, now removed, declined to comment.

Dustin was put ashore at the next port, his lifeboat suite officially closed for business.
